groups.question: Why does the body need carbon dioxide?
texts:
It mostly doesn't. The whole thing is a side effect of how you get rid of it. You end up with too much of the gas from burning off your cells and the only way to keep your blood from getting too alkaline is to keep it in a state of equilibrium. Your kidneys can buffer it, and your lungs can blow it off, and the whole arrangement keeps your pH where your proteins will still work. You actually would stop breathing if that level ever got to be too low because your brain is watching the pH to figure out when to take in more air. It mistakes the resulting fall in acidity for a shortage of oxygen.

You do end up using it to make the bicarbonate that serves as that buffer but that is just the mechanism for its disposal. If you for instance got that all out of your system in a hurry you would wind up in a state where your heart started acting very badly. That is the closest you'll get to a need.

It mostly doesn't. You get far more than you need from your own cellular respiration. That said, if you stripped every trace of it out you'd run into a couple of problems. Red blood cells use the CO2 you give them to swap bicarbonate for chloride, and they can't keep that going without it. Lose that and the blood's acid balance goes out the window. The bicarbonate buffer system that keeps your pH in the right ballpark also has a CO2 end that it depends on.

It acts as a local signal for the blood vessels in your brain to open up and send in more flow. You can actually get into a bad state of constriction if you put someone on pure oxygen and cut off the CO2 they normally have to work with.

You wouldn't want to go out and deliberately inhale it, though. You already make more than enough for every one of these jobs to get done.

You mostly get it for free as a result of burning glucose, but a fair bit of your plumbing depends on it. The obvious piece is the Bohr effect, where CO2 makes hemoglobin let go of the oxygen it is carrying. That grip loosens exactly in the tissues that are making it, which turns your blood into a rather smart delivery system. If you kept the whole thing perfectly free of the gas that would just stop working. You also need it to keep your blood from getting too alkaline, since the main buffer system in there runs on the balance between CO2 and bicarbonate. Get rid of every bit of it and the pH runs away.

You also end up with a very lame set of warning systems. Your brain in the medulla is watching the CO2 level and the matching shift in acidity far more than it is your oxygen. That is part of why low oxygen can get quite advanced before you feel any strong urge to fix it.

You mostly just need it to get out of the way. Your cells make a hell of a lot of it as a byproduct of burning sugar, and if it built up the acid in your blood would cook you. The red cells grab it and turn it into bicarbonate, which keeps the whole thing at a workable pH. You also use the resulting drop in pH to tell your brain it is time to take another breath. Breathe in pure oxygen with none of that gas in the mix and those sensors might well decide you are fine and stop.

It does change how well your blood carries oxygen too. The presence of the gas helps hemoglobin let go of its cargo in the working muscles. That part works out fine so long as you keep up a normal level of the stuff. Strip it away and you are left with a couple of pretty nasty chemical imbalances.

It's mostly a waste product you'd just want to get rid of. The trouble is you can't get rid of all of it. Your blood has a buffering system that leans on CO2 to keep the pH from getting too high. You lose that acid and a bunch of stuff starts to misbehave. Your muscles get all twitchy, your breathing goes haywire, and the part of your brain that keeps you taking breaths gets all confused. You've got a lot of enzymes and proteins that flat out refuse to work outside that narrow band.

It helps that the stuff you make is so reactive with water. You end up with carbonic acid and a bunch of bicarbonate and that pair does a lot of the heavy lifting to keep the whole thing in balance. So you keep around the very thing you are trying to dump. You just have to keep it from getting too concentrated.

Most of it is just garbage you have to get rid of. Your cells burn sugar and oxygen to get energy and end up with CO2 as the exhaust. If you kept that in the blood it would turn into carbonic acid and your pH would drop to a level your enzymes can't handle. You need to keep enough of it around though to stop that same system from swinging the other way and making the blood too alkaline. You'll actually feel pretty lousy if you end up breathing air that is 100 percent oxygen and has none of it.

It also changes how your red blood cells behave. Hemoglobin lets go of its oxygen more easily in the presence of CO2, which is convenient since that is exactly where the exhaust is being made. You would end up with a pretty bad mismatch of what tissues need if that connection got broken. So you are forced to keep an amount of the waste product in the system just to keep a few other things running right.

It's mostly a matter of your blood's chemistry. Your cells dump out hydrogen ions as a side effect of making energy and you have to get rid of them. Your kidneys and lungs team up to do this and the whole system runs on the carbon you breathe out. The CO2 ends up as bicarbonate, which acts as a shock absorber to keep your pH from swinging around. Give someone a tube to breathe through a wind that blows away their exhaled gas and their blood will get so alkaline they get dizzy and can't get enough oxygen.

You also see the effect in the Bohr effect. The local build up of the gas helps force oxygen out of your hemoglobin so the tissues can get it. Without that little push the whole process would be far less efficient. You'd probably get by for a spell with almost none of it but the internal balance would collapse pretty quickly.

It's mostly a matter of getting oxygen out of your blood. The hemoglobin that carries oxygen grabs on to it too tightly to let go where you need it. A little bit of CO2 makes that hemoglobin let go, which is why you'll pass out in a pure oxygen atmosphere. You also need it to keep your blood from going too alkaline. The whole thing runs on a pretty tight see saw and taking the CO2 out breaks the balance. You end up with blood that is far too basic to keep the other enzymes working right.

You are of course constantly making the stuff as a waste product from your cells. You are just keeping that waste on hand because the rest of the machinery won't run without it. It is a bit like a car that needs a certain amount of exhaust backflow to run in the first place.

groups.question: If it's illegal to not have auto-insurance, why doesn't the government control and regulate auto-insurance as a Tax, rather than letting private companies sell you a mandatory service?
texts:
You can get a lot of the same effect without the government pricing everything out. Most states already tell you exactly what you have to be able to pay for, they just leave the pricing to a bunch of competing companies. You get to choose between them and those companies have a pretty detailed handle on your own risk. A state bureau would have a much harder time working out those individual odds. It's a little like how they license the doctors and set the rules for surgery, but leave the actual fees to the market. That's a lot less machinery to keep in motion.

You'd also be stuck with a single price list for everybody which would end up penalizing the careful drivers to make up for the worst ones. Right now a clean record will still get you out of paying the going rate. You probably wouldn't be all that comfortable with the government sitting down to sort out every one of those finer points.

You don't actually have to buy the service from any one provider. You can shop among a bunch of licensed carriers to get the cheapest one that meets the minimum. That's a market with a floor put under it. You have that same freedom with worker's comp on the contractor's side. What you'd get out of a state run plan is the exact opposite. Without private companies competing for your business the pricing would get stuck and the only thing you'd have left to complain about would be the amount.

You see it all the time with state employees retirement systems. The lack of outside pricing information ends up letting the present costs keep ratcheting up. A single giant buyer isn't going to stop that from happening. It will probably just lock the thing in. You'd end up with neither the flexibility of the current system nor the efficiency that competition is supposed to bring about.

It's mostly a matter of who ends up paying the bill. Under the current setup the private company takes the hit when you wreck somebody's car. You pay that company out of pocket and they front the repair. If the state took it on it would actually be a sort of self insured system funded by everybody. You'd get a big chunk of that back if you never got in an accident, but that's too complicated for the folks who handle the revenue. They'd just have to keep the whole thing in a giant and very inflexible pot.

That said you are getting a pretty bad deal right now anyway. The state has the power to force you to buy the product and that tends to drive up the price. The private companies know they are guaranteed a customer so they can charge a whole lot more than they would be able to get away with in an actually competitive setup. You've got the best of both for them which is to say the worst of both for you. Something along the lines of the British National Health Service has tried to solve this exact snafu and it has ended up creating enough fresh problems that people in that system are guaranteed to grumble about it.

It's mostly a numbers game. Figuring out what to charge you and your neighbor is a nightmare of risk management. They'd have to stare at a whole bunch of local driving records to get the odds right. If they got that wrong they'd end up with a massive deficit or a bunch of people getting shut out. The private mills can screw that up and then just die off, which messes up the state outfit a lot less. You already have this setup for a bunch of other things. Nobody lets you run a restaurant until you've got a health certificate, the city just checks the paperwork and doesn't go out to cook the meals itself.

You'd also lose the only real check you've got on their rates. When the state is the only game in town they have no real reason to keep their own prices from creeping up. You'd almost certainly end up stuck with a one size fits all price that would leave some people paying way too much. That doesn't necessarily help anyone who can't afford the bill in the first place.

You could do it and a bunch of countries do. You'd probably end up with lower rates since you are scraps the profit margin the private companies build in. The main thing that stops it here is the political fight over what the rates should be. You get the same pricing fights you get with private companies but you have to drag them out in a legislature where the whole thing gets held up by every special interest. The private companies at least make those adjustments without having to get a statute passed.

It is mostly just that nobody in the various states has managed to get a coherent single plan through the whole tangle. It is a patchwork from an awful lot of earlier and mostly unrelated decisions. You probably wouldn't build the system out that way if you were starting over from nothing.

You can do that and some countries do, Germany has a scheme where one national fund fronts the payment. But you still end up with wildly different prices since the fund prices each car by its actual odds of getting into an accident. You'd just be paying a variable levy to the state instead of a monthly premium to some firm. Calling it a tax wouldn't get you a flat rate either. You are just moving the billing function to a different set of hands.

You also lose the ability to shop anywhere you might get a better deal. Once they have a monopoly they have zero incentive to keep the administration lean. Most of the people who have looked into the idea figure it just ends up adding a new layer of cost on top of what you are already paying.

You're mostly comparing two different animals. A tax just sweeps up a cut to pay for things like fixing the roads you drive on. You don't get anything back in return for the money itself. The bet you are making with an insurance policy is that if you wreck your car somebody will front the cash to get you back on the road. Getting the state to underwrite every single one of those gambles gets to be a nightmarish job for the administrators. It isn't impossible since lots of states already run their own plug in plans for people the private sector won't touch. You can also get out of buying the product entirely if you can come up with a huge sum of cash to stand in its place. Most people look at that alternative and end up paying the private companies for the favor anyway.

You mostly can't get out from under the private side without tearing a pretty big chunk of the existing system out. The patchwork you see now is a product of state by state tinkering that the big companies have had a lot of say in. You also run into a real headache trying to price things out of the market. The companies get away with charging a lot more for the high risk crowd by balancing that out with rock bottom prices for the rest. A flat tax would leave you with either a giant loss or rates that nobody could swallow. You get a look at what that sort of thing looks like in a number of the northern states that gave it a try. They all ran into the same kind of financial pinches you'd get in a big state.

On top of that you have to think about the sheer muscle the industry has put in over the years. Pulling that out of the picture is a lot harder than it looks. You manage to do it and you have to cover the whole thing out of a central fund. That ends up looking an awful lot like you are taking the losses of the unlucky and spreading them around to everybody. Plenty of people will tell you that makes the whole thing impossible to get through a legislature to begin with.

They've set up a choice between "government runs it as a tax" and "private companies sell a mandatory service" as though those were the only two options. They aren't. The actual system in most US states is that the government sets the minimum coverage you must carry and then lets private companies compete to provide it. You could get the same mandatory-service outcome from a government monopoly, or you could let the state compete against private ones. Neither of those is what's happening.

The tax comparison also gets the mechanics wrong. You pay a tax to the government for some public good. You pay a premium to a company that is then liable to make you whole if you wreck something. The private company isn't selling you some abstract government service, it's taking on a specific financial risk that the state has decided you must be able to meet.

You could also point out that the whole thing is much less efficient if the government tried to price out every individual accident risk. Private companies have a fair amount of information about your driving that a single state bureau would find very difficult to make use of.

You'd get a big chunk of that back if you never got in an accident, but that's too complicated for the folks who handle the revenue. That said you are getting a pretty bad deal right now anyway. The state has the power to force you to buy the product and that tends to drive up the price. The private companies know they are guaranteed a customer so they can charge a whole lot more than they would be able to get away with in an actually competitive setup. You've got the best of both for them which is to say the worst of both for you. Something along the lines of the British National Health Service has tried to solve this exact snafu and it has ended up creating enough fresh problems that people in that system are guaranteed to grumble about it.

You get the same thing with lots of other mandates like building codes or food safety rules. You have to get a building permit, but the city doesn't then go out and build your house for you. The rules just have to be satisfied in some way. The private market ends up filling that role.

I'm guessing they also have a somewhat idealized picture of how government provision would work. You'd likely see a huge administrative apparatus just trying to figure out what is fair to charge different people. You'd also lose the competition that keeps the private rates from getting too high. If the state were the only game in town, there wouldn't really be much to keep them in check. You'd probably end up with a whole lot of people losing coverage they actually needed since they wouldn't be able to get out from under the state rates. It's mostly a numbers game. Figuring out what to charge you and your neighbor is a nightmare of risk management. They'd have to stare at a whole bunch of local driving records to get the odds right. If they got that wrong they'd end up with a massive deficit or a bunch of people getting shut out. The private mills can screw that up and then just die off, which messes up the state outfit a lot less. You already have this setup for a bunch of other things. Nobody lets you run a restaurant until you've got a health certificate, the city just checks the paperwork and doesn't go out to cook the meals itself.

You'd also lose the only real check you've got on their rates. When the state is the only game in town they have no real reason to keep their own prices from creeping up. You'd almost certainly end up stuck with a one size fits all price that would leave some people paying way too much. That doesn't necessarily help anyone who can't afford the bill in the first place.

You get to avoid the profit margin built into private rates, and you don't have to shop. A lot of countries actually do run state monopolies or at least heavily regulated public options. The US is the main outlier among rich countries in this regard.

That said the whole thing runs into some pretty practical difficulties. You need to know fairly precisely the risk each individual driver poses and tweaking that in a single big pool is a real headache. You also end up with a public entity that has to constantly fight over its own pricing and terms in the political arena. Private competition at least forces some of that adjustment to happen without a legislative fight.

Nobody really has a clean answer to all of this and the US system is mostly the result of historical accidents in how the various state legislatures got around to the issue. You end up with this patchwork that nobody would design if starting in from scratch. The question is perfectly reasonable even if the practical answer is that the sausage gets made in a lot of different and not very pretty ways.

You could do it and a bunch of countries do. You'd probably end up with lower rates since you are scraps the profit margin the private companies build in. The main thing that stops it here is the political fight over what the rates should be. You get the same pricing fights you get with private companies but you have to drag them out in a legislature where the whole thing gets held up by every special interest. The private companies at least make those adjustments without having to get a statute passed.

It is mostly just that nobody in the various states has managed to get a coherent single plan through the whole tangle. It is a patchwork from an awful lot of earlier and mostly unrelated decisions. You probably wouldn't build the system out that way if you were starting over from nothing.

The end result for most people would look a lot the same. You'd still get hit with higher prices for being a risk. You also lose the ability to shop anywhere you might get a better deal. Once they have a monopoly they have zero incentive to keep the administration lean. Most of the people who have looked into the idea figure it just ends up adding a new layer of cost on top of what you are already paying.

The state would have to underwrite every single policy, which is an absolutely massive operational headache. Getting the state to underwrite every single one of those gambles gets to be a nightmarish job for the administrators. It isn't impossible since lots of states already run their own plug in plans for people the private sector won't touch. You can also get out of buying the product entirely if you can come up with a huge sum of cash to stand in its place. Most people look at that alternative and end up paying the private companies for the favor anyway.

groups.question: if a human embryo isn't viable, by what mechanism does the body decide to terminate? What is it that goes "this isn't working, scrap it"?
texts:
There isn't a little overseer looking the whole thing over. You've got a couple of things that work out that way for you. Your ovaries hang off the hCG the embryo is supposed to be pumping out. That is the only signal your pituitary gets to keep the corpus luteum alive. If you don't get a sufficient amount of that hormone back the corpus luteum just withers and stops making progesterone. Without that the lining of your womb can't hold on and gets shed. It's a lot like pulling a plug on a tank. You don't have to send in anyone to empty it.

You also have a local test that is effectively all or nothing. The cells in that lining either manage to establish a blood supply that can keep up with the things they are trying to become or they do not. A big chunk of the errors you run into are chromosomal and the cells just can't divide in a way that gets them past that point. If you got the bad draw in the oviduct you might just get it expelled on the way back. That part of the tube is too narrow to support anything that has gotten too far along to turn around. The whole thing amounts to a series of supports simply failing to get put in place.

You are mostly watching a bunch of mechanical failures rather than some sort of decision getting made. The vast majority of the time it's that the thing was put together with the wrong chromosomes in the first place. It builds itself out to a point and then just stops. You hit a wall somewhere around the seventh week because the placenta never got the right instructions to take over.

That failure to take over sends the hCG readings back down. The corpus luteum in the ovary reads that as a signal to stop pumping out progesterone. Without that hormone the endometrium will no longer maintain itself. The uterine muscle just goes about the normal part of the cycle that it would have done anyway had you not gotten pregnant. You end up expelling the thing pretty much the same way you shed a normal monthly lining. Some of that local rejection gets kicked off in the very earliest stages by the immune system noticing that an implantation took the wrong course. You are probably getting that sort of thing done on a pretty regular basis without ever noticing it.

Nobody is really making a call. It's more like a set of mechanical dependencies failing in sequence. The embryo sends out trophoblast cells to get a foothold in the uterine wall. Those cells are also what keep the corpus luteum pumping out progesterone. If the embryo is misshapen or has some chromosomal screw up the cells can't get a proper hold. That means the progesterone supply dries up. Once that happens the endometrium just breaks down and gets shed in what is functionally a very heavy period. You get the corpse out more or less for free.

You'd see something very similar in a root canal. Once the nerve dies the tooth is just as much a dead end as the nonviable pregnancy. The body has no particular interest in keeping either one around once the internal machinery to support them has stopped working. It simply lets the whole thing come apart.

You've got it mostly right in that there isn't some central judge. It's a stack of interlocking requirements and when one of them stops getting met the whole thing comes apart. For the first several weeks the whole thing is held together by the corpus luteum keeping the uterine lining in place. That keeps it going only as long as the embryo keeps sending back enough hCG. That signal stops and the corpus luteum just dies off and the lining sheds. It looks a lot like a period and is for the most part just that.

You get some extra help from the immune system in the form of what you might see as the body recognizing and getting rid of damaged tissue. The normal suppression of that response also depends on signals from the embryo so when those stop the defenses act. And then you have the same muscular machinery that will eventually expel a full term child. Prostaglandins that get released in the wake of the damage set the contractions going.

So the termination ends up looking a lot like a failure to maintain the very conditions the thing needed to continue. There's no one there to look at the results and say it must be scrapped.

You've got a bit of a ghost in the machine there. There's no central point that runs a quality check and stamps a rejection. It's mostly a chain of contingencies that only holds together while things are on track. The embryo is supposed to send out hCG to tell the corpus luteum to keep pouring out progesterone, and that progesterone is what keeps the endometrium from breaking down. Miss the mark on chromosomes and you get too little of that signal. The corpus luteum then does what it always was going to do in the absence of that signal, it withers. The lining sloughs off and the whole thing comes away. You'd get the same result from a lot of other things that just failed to produce enough of the chemical prop.

You do get a little inflammatory response on top of that, which nags at the uterine muscle and gets it to push things out. That part can look a lot like a deliberate act of repair. But it's more like the house getting swept out by the wind after the supporting walls fall. The sweeping isn't because someone made up their mind the house had to go.

Nobody is running the check. It's mostly a failure of the implantation site to get a big enough blood supply. You've got a very narrow window in the uterine lining where it's set up to take on the growing embryo. Keep giving it the right chemical signals, mostly a particular balance of hCG. If the embryo is out of shape chromosomally it generally stops producing the required inputs somewhere around two weeks in. The local tissue just stops getting what it needs, the little implant ends up sloughing off, and the regular muscle action of the uterus deals with it. You get the same sort of inflammatory clearance you'd get for any bit of dead tissue that has to be got rid of. Almost all of these cases are just the genetic code being unable to keep up with the very next step in development. The machinery then backs out of a relationship it never got to complete.

You'll see similar things happen in vitro fertilization work, where you can track the exact points where these chemical signals fail to get through. The whole thing ends up looking more like a series of necessary conditions going unmet than some sort of centralCleanup operation.

There isn't really a committee getting together to vote. Most of the time the whole thing just runs out of the signals it needs to keep going. The embryo has to keep pumping out hcg to stop the corpus luteum from dying. That little gland is the only thing making the progesterone and estrogen that hold the uterine lining together. Fail to make enough hcg and the gland withers, the hormones run out, and the next thing that happens is the lining being sloughed off. That's just the menstrual cycle happening, same as it would have on schedule. You are getting what in effect is a late and probably heavier period. You don't get a separate "scrap it" mechanism, you just lose the mechanism that was artificially holding that process at bay.

On top of that the decidual cells that form around the implant site have their own programs for breaking down, and the prostaglandins they release in that process end up driving the contractions. There is an immune response in the mix too though nobody has fully sorted out how much that contributes. You can get in a bit of trouble by the way things went wrong and when that happened. A chromosomal snag at the very earliest stages simply fails to set up the signal chain in the first place. The end result is the same either way though. No continuing instruction to keep the system in a pregnant state.

It's mostly just the absence of a go ahead signal. Right after you get pregnant your corpus luteum is dumping out progesterone to keep the uterine lining in repair. That thing will only keep it up as long as it keeps getting hit with hCG from the developing placenta. If the development has gone wrong the hCG never gets high enough. The corpus luteum winds up dying off, the hormones drop, and the lining breaks down and gets shed. You get a menses that ends up looking a lot like a miscarriage. There is no inspector going around to determine that something has gone astray. The whole thing just collapses for lack of the confirming input.

That said a whole lot of the time the thing that keeps the hCG from being made in the first place is some internal chromosomal problem. The thing just can't get far enough along to put out the required chemistry. Vaginal peristalsis will also in some cases simply expel a very early and inadequate implantation. But in the end the whole process is more a case of the support system failing to get a continuation order than anyone actively carrying out a culling.

There's also a lot of local stuff going on. Decidual cells surrounding the implant site have their own apoptotic programs. If things aren't right they'll break down and help expel the contents. The prostaglandins that get released as the lining breaks down are also what cause the uterine contractions. You get a bit of an immune component to it as well, though the exact contribution of that is still something people are working out.

Most of the time nothing complicated happens. You just get what looks like a late or heavy period. The more dramatic scenarios people picture are actually the less common ones.

It's worth mentioning that the exact point at which things go wrong varies quite a bit. Chromosomal problems in the very early stages tend to just prevent the embryo from establishing the signal chain. Later on you can have a range of issues. The end result is the same though. No sustained signal, no continued support, and the system reverts to what it was doing before.

groups.question: Why do tickets dispensed by arcade machines always seem to arrange themselves into neat piles?
texts:
It's mostly an artifact of every ticket being forced down the same path. Out the back there's a spring that keeps pushing the next one forward, and the slot they have to get out of is narrow enough to line them up. The result is that shingled stack you see, each one poking out a little from the last. That is pretty much as neat as the arrangement is ever going to get. Give it enough time and you've got a solid lump you can't get a ticket out of. You'd get a far worse mess if you were just raking through a jar. The brain is pretty good at finding a pattern in that arrangement and calling it order though.

You'd get something very different from the coin return in a slot machine. They dump a random assortment of coins and since all of them are the same size that random assortment looks a lot less interesting. You still end up with a pile, it just doesn't line up anywhere near as nicely.

Most of it is the slot doing the work. You pull the short end out first and the long end trails behind, then the thing's own weight drops it into the same orientation. Get the next one out the same way and it just lands on top. Do that forty or fifty times and you've got a stack without having to sort a thing. You'd get exactly the same result pulling a bunch of plastic straws out of a tube. The neat pile is an illusion that only shows up once you've got a fair quantity of them in hand.

The long thin shape helps a lot since there's very little of each ticket sticking out to the sides. A pile of say playing cards would get all gimmick in the same way, you just wouldn't keep the rest of them so well. You almost certainly knocked the edges into line as you were carrying them off to the redemption counter.

It's a bit of a screw trick. Inside the tube there's a long helical auger, kind of like what you'd see in an old inkwell. As it shoves a ticket out the end, the spiral forces the ticket to rotate. Then the fixed inside of the tube smooths out whatever shape it was in when you put it in. Every single ticket leaves that way, with the same curl and the same rotation. The last thing they hit is a little rib or something that stops the rotation, and then they just drop onto the one in front of them. You could even stuff in a handful of crumpled receipts and get the same tidy result at the other end.

You'd never guess that from the outside. It looks like the whole contraption was built for the express purpose of making things orderly. Same mechanism is in the ticket machines at nearly every fair going back to who knows when. You'd probably see a more haphazard pile if the auger were turned the other way, but nobody has much of a use for that.

It's mostly just the machine being a bit of a cheapskate with its construction. You've got a slot built to just barely fit the width of the tickets, and there's a little spring or flap in there to bump each new one along. That trick lines them all up the same way so they end up in a stack. If the thing were just going to dump a disordered mess of little strips you would find yourself constantly picking out the first one by hand. You'd see far more of that in the little bin at the back of the contraption where the occasional badly cut ticket has to be pulled out. What you see up front is just the result of a lot of little uniform operations getting bunched together.

You're mostly seeing the result of dropping a bunch of things in exactly the same spot. The tickets get cut to one narrow width so they line up, then the little lip on the machine funnels them out one at a time. The next one lands on the first, nudging it back into line, kind of the way you'd get if you dropped a pile of playing cards from the same height. It's also your brain doing a fair amount of work to see a pattern. Look long enough and you'll find plenty of them that are askew, you just jump right over those.

You get the same effect with any number of very uniform objects. Pour out a box of matches from the same place and you'll end up with neat little strips too. If you tried the same thing with a bunch of receipts you'd have a far more interesting and far less orderly mess on your hands.

You're seeing the machine's own doing. The little prism that prints the numbered face rolls the next ticket forward in a locked together stack. That whole group is then forced through a chute that is only just wide enough to let them through. The first one hits the little stop at the end and the rest get shunted in behind it one at a time. You'd get the same thing out of a change machine since the internal mechanism is shoving a full stack around. The whole thing would fall apart only if you batted at it.

If you were to take a single one off that group the ones behind it would have to adjust their own position. That just doesn't happen fast enough to mess up the remaining group. It is hardly a mystery of self arranging matter, it is only the machine dragging its whole parcel through in exactly the shape it had before.

It's mostly the slot they come out of. It's narrow enough that the tickets can't really go left or right as they get pushed out. Add in the fact that they're printed on fairly heavy stock, and you get a stack pretty much for free. They don't so much arrange themselves as they never had any chance to get out of line. You'd get something very similar if you dropped a deck of cards through a tight tube. You'll still get a bit of fan out in the end, you can't really get rid of that, but the first impression is of a tidy pile.

They also come out one at a time in fairly quick succession. If you got a big wad all at once the thing would almost certainly end up in a mess. The little pause between each ticket gives the last one a chance to settle on top of the one before it.

You are more likely to ruin the pile by grabbing it than the machine ever was to get it wrong.

It's mostly just the slot doing the work. You've got a narrow deep opening and every ticket gets shoved out of it in exactly the same orientation. They land right on top of the one before them and the friction between their surfaces keeps them from sliding around. No hidden sorting is going on, it's simply that you can't get much sideways motion out of that particular geometry. You'll see the same effect from pretty much any machine that pushes out a string of small identical parts.

The effect does fall apart if you get a really big batch though. Gravity will eventually get the edges to creep out and you end up with a lopsided mess. But for the handful you're usually handed the stack looks almost too perfectly ordered to be the result of so little control. You are basically attributing to some sort of outside magic what is really just a pretty tight set of physical constraints.

groups.question: How can you "feel" someone behind or near you?
texts: It is almost always your brain over reading a lot of tiny data. You hear a footstep or a cough and instantly build an idea of who is out there. The smell of perfume or the flash of a strange shadow works the same way. Your eyes are pretty good at catching movement out of the corner of your view too. There is a part of the visual system wired to send off an alarm on that sort of input. That alarm gets your body to whip around, and what you then see fills in the rest of the story. It works well enough that it feels like you have some kind of direct perception. Ninety times out of a hundred you end up looking at nothing but a stray branch or the wind. The thing that feels like a distinct sense is just a very old and very conservative set of habits.

You are picking up on a bunch of really faint sensory cues. You get a tiny sound that you can't place, maybe a shift in the air, or some kind of peripheral motion. Your ears and eyes take in that kind of information so readily that your brain will run with it. Since you are naturally on the lookout for trouble the thing to do is to jump to the only conclusion you have. That little story you put together in your head is something you then take to be fact.

You get left with the impression that you have some kind of radar. It is not that actually. You just remember the rare times when the guess turned out to be right. All the times the guess was wrong you simply overlook. If you tried to test the thing under controlled conditions you would find the whole thing to be quite evasive. It ends up being a pretty comfortable and easy way to deal with not knowing what is out there.

You've got a ridiculous amount of light sensitive stuff in the corners of your eyes. Those parts of your vision are really bad at making out details but they are great at flagging that something moved. You dart your head over to check and see nothing, and your brain files it away as some kind of person. You get a lot of the same trouble from your hearing since it's so hard to pin down the exact direction of a faint sound. You also pick up the very faint warmth of a body standing close to you through the skin.

None of that requires any sort of sixth sense though. You are just remembering the few times your guesses happened to come true while you forget the long run of false alarms. You are also entirely free to attach any kind of spooky story to the raw stuff your senses send up. Your brain is perfectly content to fill in the gaps with whatever it thinks you might have seen.

It's mostly your ears and the corners of your eyes doing the work. Your eyes pick up a shifting patch of light or a broken shadow way out in the distance. At the same time your ears start sorting the local sounds to see if any of them has the right rhythm or pitch to be a person. Your brain just takes that thin scrap of data and invents a whole person to account for it. That little cold feeling you get is mostly the same thing, your muscles getting ready to run from a danger you only half made up.

That whole process falls apart the moment you are in a crowd. Too many moving sounds and shapes are around to tell you who is actually there. Even the quiet of an empty street gives you plenty of false alarms. You are almost certainly wrong about the cause of that last twinge and that is the basis for the whole thing. You have just got really good at making a story out of very little to keep you from being taken by surprise.

You're catching a few different things and your brain is stitching them into a single sense of presence. Your ears are better at locating sound behind you than in front, and they pick up the particular sounds a person makes. You get a rustle of clothing, a change in the local air current, or the faint sound of breathing. At the same time the edge of your vision is constantly scanning for the kind of movement a body would make. Your mind has an enormous stock of past experience to work with and it uses that to fill in the picture. You have the feeling of a person being there and then you turn to look for the evidence.

You'll also find that this system makes a bunch of errors. You get the same jolt from a tree branch in the wind or a stray cat. That says a lot about what you are actually sensing. It is just your own very good at guessing pattern matching machinery that has been trained to expect a person to be there. The feeling comes first and the fact comes later if it comes at all.

You are mostly getting hit by a bunch of tiny inputs your brain then stitches into a story. You might catch a faint click, some slight change in the air, or the smallest bit of air pressure on your skin. None of that amounts to proof of someone being there. Your mind just builds a little scenario out of the raw data and slaps a fact label on it. It feels like a genuine sense because it happens all at once. Turn around to find you are alone and you will probably write the whole thing off. The next time the same patchwork of odd happenings lines up though you will almost certainly have the same conviction.

You get just the same sort of thing out of a whole lot of listening. Your ears can't split two notes of exactly the same pitch. That inability makes all sorts of background noise sound like a distinct and nearby presence. You are forever guessing at the direction such a sound is coming from too. Get the guess wrong and you will end up convinced that some person is standing in quite the wrong part of the room. The result is a very convincing phantom that is nothing more than your own doing.

You get most of it from your ears. The outside of your head blocks and distorts sound in a way that your brain is good at reading for stuff in front of you. From behind that same distortion ends up looking a bit like a general and very vivid impression. Your brain then fills in the rest with an almost visual picture. Your peripheral vision is also constantly picking up on shadows and moving shapes. It is notoriously bad at getting the actual shape of the thing and hands that information off to your expectations to sort out. If you already expect to be attacked those very same impressions will to you like someone is actually there.

You are also picking up on a whole set of changes in the air that your own movement would normally cause. A person in that area alters the temperature and flow of that air in a way that you register without being consciously aware of it. You have probably had plenty of occasions where the thing you so clearly sensed turned out to be nothing at all. It is just your system playing it very much on the safe side.

It is mostly your own brain getting all worked up. There is a whole lot of sensitive nerve endings in the base of your neck and right over the shoulder blades. Get the least bit of wind on them or have a bit of stray hair blow in that direction and the lot of it goes off. Your brain is a habitual pattern matcher and it will scream danger up to you the minute it spots something it thinks is a threat. You get a full on startle in response to that whether there is actually a threat or not.

If you put yourself in a situation where there are lots of things that could be out there in the dark the whole thing pretty much takes off by its own power. groups.question: How do owners of non-profit organizations or people who are "experts" in really odd things make money? Are most of them just retired or do they get paid by someone to do these things?
texts:
Most of them get paid out of the fees the thing they run charges. A little museum charges for admission and that adds up to a salary for the guy running it. You're seeing the salary and skipping over the revenue that gets paid out. Same with a lot of the smaller arts and society groups, they sell something and hand the proceeds along. You've also got grant money, where you write a proposal and some foundation or government body writes you a check to do a specific thing. That last bit is a fair amount of the whole pie.

The weird experts are usually tethered to some university, and the school gets its own outside funding. That funding ends up in the form of a salary for the very specialized person. At that point it looks a lot like a retirement, since the money is more or less guaranteed, but there is still an outside source for it. A few of them can also pick up consulting work from anyone who happens to need that particular brand of help. You're probably seeing a fair bit of that consulting and just not seeing the arrangements that put it in place.

It's mostly a mix of the two you're guessing at, plus a fair amount of grant writing. If the person put a big chunk of personal money in as an endowment, the interest on that stuff ends up running the whole show. The person can then kind of ride that out. You'll also see a lot of these hyper specialists getting picked up by a university to run a small collection. They get a salary and some lab space in exchange for keeping the thing going. Book deals and the occasional lecture tour help out too, since the weirdness is exactly what the public wants to pay to see.

That said the whole thing usually still hinges on some prior fortune. You can't write your way into running a museum dedicated to some particularly obscure subject. The salaries and grants that keep the lights on almost always presuppose that somebody has already come up with a hell of a lot of cash to get it off the ground in the first place. So your retired person guess is a pretty good one for the top end of that sort of thing.

You're mostly going to find the same boring machinery in both cases. The non profit stuff runs on a pile of grants from foundations, which is to say other people have made and saved large sums of money. The people running the place will hew out a modest regular salary from that pile. You'll get a little more from membership fees if the group has those, and a scattering of individual donations. None of it looks like one guy writing a fat check.

The weird experts are a bit different. The common case is that they are professors and the university's general research pot picks up the tab. You are watching regular academic funding function in a way your eyes find striking. A smaller group get to make a living on public speaking and the odd book deal. Chances are you are seeing some of that too. It does happen that you will come across a person who has saved enough in a prior life to work on what they like. But you are probably wrong to think that is the whole story.

You mostly get paid the same way you would anywhere else. A guy running some hyper local moot court is going to take his salary out of the same pot that does, say, a fifty percent state grant, an operating award from a foundation or two, and the entrance fees his members pay. You can run that whole show without any single person acting as a patron. The one thing you can't do is divvy out of that pot in the form of a profit. It has to stay inside the thing you're running.

That odd subject matter crowd has a more patchwork situation. You will get a consulting fee here or a talk fee there plus maybe a little from writing. None of those on its own might get you to a living. So you end up stitching four or five of them together. There are a decent number of the people you see in that role who also have a pension or some funds set aside. That lets them get by on a pretty modest income from the work itself. That particular arrangement gets talked about more than it actually occurs though, which is what probably gets you to the conclusion that nearly everybody in the situation is on a retirement. A fair share of them are simply juggling a regular occupation on the side.

It's a mixed bag. The really well known ones are usually living off a big endowment that some trust or family set up. You live off the interest on that pot and it keeps you in a kind of salary. That's how a lot of university attached research groups get by. Outside of that you've got the constant grind of writing grant proposals. You get a few years of funding to do your thing and then you have to go get the next chunk. It works well enough if the weirdness you're studying can be shoehorned into a foundation's stated mission.

You do run into some people who have simply chosen to live on their own savings. They take a much smaller cut to keep the operation afloat. And the odd one out who gets some kind of oddly specific stipend from a sympathetic government body. The more off the wall your subject the harder that last bit gets though. Foundations tend to want to look like they know what they are doing.

So no there isn't some single retirement plan behind it. You are just juggling whatever scraps of institutional support you can wrangle.

You usually end up with a patchwork of all of it. The grant money you can get is often tied to very specific projects you have to write out a whole case for. The private admirers who might chip in are a small and unreliable group. So a lot of the time you are running on a pension or some other accumulated wealth you have left over. I've seen plenty of the really deep niche stuff get done that way. It is a lot of work to keep the whole thing going given that none of the individual sources tend to be enough.

You do occasionally hit on a situation where a foundation happens to be very interested in your particular subject. When that happens it can cover the bills for a spell. That situation is far from the rule though and it never quite becomes a dependable way to get by.

You're mostly right that some outside party is footin the bill. They just do it in a bunch of different ways. You'll find these folks attached to a university where they get a regular salary to do their very strange work. That is functionally the same as being hired by someone else, you just get it through an academic appointment. A lot of it also comes from foundation grants written out for a specific project. That is someone paying you to do the thing, they are just doing it in chunks and with a bunch of extra red tape. You will find the retired hobbyist in there too but you almost never see that as the only thing keeping an operation alive.

The actual setup is too much of a patchwork to divide into those first two categories. The guy who spends his life arguing about the correct way to address rural post offices is getting by on some unpaid position at a college. The lady who has devoted her whole career to keeping some extinct language from getting forgotten has to go out and chase donors every few years. You end up with a lot of these people having to cobble a living together from several different pots.

You'll usually find a pretty messy patchwork. The org might get a salary for the leader out of the general donations it takes in. You can do this for a long time without ever having a single person paying the whole bill. But you are of course still at the mercy of the people who write those checks. You end up doing a great deal of the your own time looking for that next chunk. You might get a little from one foundation and a little from another until you have enough to go on.

The odd experts you are talking about live in the same sort of situation. You might end up getting a few thousand from a book deal here and a lecture there. None of that adds up to a fortune by itself. The way it works is you have to have a fairly broad band of small time backers. It isn't so much that a boss is footing the bill as that a very large audience of people are each chipping in a bit. You never really get to the point of being entirely free of that.

It's a mixed bag. The really well known ones are usually living off a big endowment that some trust or family set up. You live off the interest on that pot and it keeps you in a kind of salary. That's how a lot of university attached research groups get by. Outside of that you've got the constant grind of writing grant proposals. You get a few years of funding to do your thing and then you have to go get the next chunk. You do run into some people who have simply chosen to live on their own savings. They take a much smaller cut to keep the operation afloat. And the odd one out who gets some kind of oddly specific stipend from a sympathetic government body. The more off the wall your subject the harder that last bit gets though. Foundations tend to want to look like they know what they are doing.

So no there isn't some single retirement plan behind it. You are just juggling whatever scraps of institutional support you can wrangle.

You do occasionally hit on a situation where a foundation happens to be very interested in your particular subject. When that happens it can cover the bills for a spell. That situation is far from the rule though and it never quite becomes a dependable way to get by.

groups.question: If residential solar is such a good investment, how come 95% percent of homes don't have it yet?
texts:
You're mostly just looking at the same thing that kept most of the country out of the car business for the first thirty years after they came out. You can't run the kit on a roof you don't own, and a big chunk of the population still rents. The sticker price also gives a lot of people pause since the payoff in most places is something like a decade out. And the whole thing gets tied up by local red tape to the point where you might be waiting a year or more for the power company to hook you in. It's working out pretty well for the ones who do get in. The ones who are still on the outside are almost always stuck on some of those practical snags rather than some fatal flaw in the underlying math for them.

That said the math is very far from automatic for any one person. It works out fantastically for a family that isn't expecting to move for the next thirty years. It's entirely possible to look at the same numbers and find you'd be better off putting that money somewhere else.

You've got the math backwards. Plenty of great investments sit unused by the vast majority of people. Difference in a stock is you only tie up a little cash and can get out any time. Solar is a huge lump sum you are stuck with. You are betting that you'll be in that same house another twenty five or thirty years. Most people change addresses way before that point. And the whole thing falls apart if your utility company decides to mess with the rates you were counting on. You end up with a system you can't conveniently take with you. That sort of long term lock up keeps it to a pretty small group.

You get a similar picture with a lot of the nationally advertised health programs. Everybody agrees they are good for you yet hardly anybody takes them up. People just don't have the will or the means to commit to something that far out.

You're mostly starting from a false premise. You've got about a two to three percent of the country with the stuff up there, not the five percent you've probably heard. The rest of the nation is largely just plain cash poor. You need a fairly huge chunk of money to get going and a great many people simply can't come up with it. On top of that you have the local red tape. The whole permit and inspection gig ends up soaking too much of the potential savings.

That returns part is also a long drawn out affair. You maybe ought to be prepared to wait more than ten years for the numbers to actually work in your favor. That's harder than it sounds to swallow for people who live from month to month. All of the legislative maneuvering you see on the news does very little to change the shape of your monthly power bill. People are quite right to leave the whole thing alone until it actually costs less to run.

It's mostly the length of time you have to stick around to see the payoff. You're looking at 25 to 30 years to recoup the cost and you're almost certainly going to move long before that. You end up selling the panels to the next owner and they are the ones who actually pocket the savings. That isn't nearly as appealing as the sales pitch makes it sound. You've got a lot of cash coming up front that you can't take with you when you leave. The only folks who end up with all the benefit are those who happen to have a place they will never leave.

You can get some of the same protection from rate increases just by going all electric with your heating and cooling, and that you can actual take along with you. That approach does not have the same kind of performance though. It doesn't so much beat the system as it keeps you from getting burned by it. The whole thing is a perfectly fine bet as long as you happen to be around to see it come in.

You're mostly getting hit by the sticker price. The math only pencils out if you can cough down a four or five figure up front and you have a roof that meets all the local requirements. Even where the incentives are pretty generous that outlay is still a non starter for most people. A lot of folks are also paying power rates low enough that the payoff drags on for decades. You then have to factor in that a bunch of the expected savings disappear if the house ends up being rented out to someone else.

It's the same situation you get with any other big ticket purchase that requires a very specific set of local conditions to make sense. The investment looks like a slam dunk in a spreadsheet but that doesn't tell you anything about whether a given neighbor can actually get in on it.

You've got the wrong figure to work with. That number is mostly a measure of how high the entry price still is rather than any hidden flaw in the long term math. You'll get a nice return on that money if you live somewhere that gets a lot of direct sun and happens to charge a high price for grid power. It's a pretty poor deal if you live in the middle of a big city where that happens to be a non issue. The terms of the local net metering plan also throw a lot of uncertainty into the whole thing. It's hard for the average person to run those numbers with enough confidence to justify such a large outlay.

You see this same pattern in a whole lot of other technologies that eventually turn out to be the smart thing to get. The people who got in early just got to be in on a set of particular local conditions that just didn't apply to the rest.

The 95 percent figure has way more to do with prerequisites than the payoff. You've got to own the place, have a roof in the right orientation, and pony up to the tune of several thousand dollars up front. On top of that you are stuck in a permitting process that shifts every time you change counties. The utility you hook into might give you a big credit for what you generate or might give you nothing. None of that is a refutation of the fact that the numbers work out, it is just true that the numbers work out for a pretty narrow slice of the population. There is also a real gap between a 20 year payoff and the way most people think about money.

That said you are seeing the rate of adoption change fairly fast in the last couple of years. The up front cost has come down a lot and a few states have set up programs to cover it without the homeowner having to front the whole sum. Those two things together are getting around most of what kept the rest of the country from getting in.

You're mostly hitting on the fact that it only works out for a pretty narrow slice of owners. You need a roof that faces the right way and gets the right amount of direct sun. You also need to be in a state where the utility will send you a real credit for the extra power. In a bunch of states that credit is worth very little or gets capped after you even out your own usage. A lot of people also get stuck on the upfront cash that the system needs. You can get around that with loans or leases, but that ends up wiping out much of the long term gain. That gain also leans heavily on a tax credit that a lot of people have nothing to offset it against.

You run into a decent amount of red tape in places with strict home owners associations too. Those groups have a way of nixing the entire setup before you get very far. Each one of these stumbling blocks is pretty easy to brush aside in a hypothetical but they add up to a list that a lot of actual homeowners can't get past.

groups.question: Why don't any larger animals have compound/multiple eyes like bugs do?
texts:
You mostly do see some of it in the ocean. Spiny lobsters and a lot of the bigger crabs run compound eyes pretty successfully. So it isn't an absolute size limit. The problem is what those eyes can do. Every little facet gives you a tiny piece of a picture and you stitch a lot of them together to get a view. You end up with a huge field and some excellent motion detection. Fine if you are a wasp or a mayfly. That whole setup hits a hard ceiling on how much sharp detail you can get though. You would have to throw on so many of the little units to see things in any more detail that the optic nerve and the bit of brain to sort it all out would get ridiculous.

A single lens gets around that problem. It puts all the light from a point onto one spot on the back of the eye. That is what gives you your fine detail. The mantis kind of gets the best of both with a pair of lens eyes set into a compound arrangement. The octopus pretty much threw the whole compound idea out in favor of a very well made focusable lens. Once you get to the size of a dog or a person, those seem to have been the only workable ways to sort of see.

It's mostly a matter of what you get out of the deal. Each of the little lenses that makes up a compound eye only sees a tiny part of the picture. Your brain then has to buzz all of that together into something you can use. Up close that gives you a gorgeous, if slightly blurry, view of pretty much everything. You lose a lot of the sharp detail that a single big lens like ours gets. That is a price a beetle can afford to pay. A lion stalking a zebra from two hundred yards out simply can't. To get any sort of detail out of that many tiny lenses you'd end up with a head the size of a dump truck.

On top of the optics you've got the wiring problem. Feeding the signals from thousands of little lenses into the brain drains a fair amount of capacity. The nervous system of a wasp is organized to handle that. Scaling it up to match the needs of a larger creature hasn't quite gotten off the ground. You do see a little of this sort of thing elsewhere. The nautilus keeps a row of fairly crude pinhole eyes and some jellyfish dot the bells with a bunch of them. None of it gets you the kind of fine stereoscopic vision a big predator is after.

It's mostly a resolution problem. Each tiny lens in a compound eye (an ommatidium) only catches a very small fuzzy bit of the scene. You end up with a wide angle view and first rate motion detection, but you can't make out fine detail. For a fly that's plenty. If a hawk tried to spy out a field mouse from a couple hundred yards off it would be useless. You'd have to pack in so many of these little lenses to get any use out of them that the whole eye would get to be an impossible size.

You do run into a couple of exceptions though. Some of the bigger crustaceans get along just fine with them, and the dragonfly sort of blends the two approaches. The fish and the cephalopods mostly stuck with the camera type eye that you and I have. Once you get big enough to need to pick out small things, the compound model just stops being useful.

groups.question: How almost every book in a bookstore is written by 'New York Times Best-Selling author'
texts:
It's mostly that there are a squandrum of lists to get on. You don't have to crack some single national ranking. Touch the fiction list, or the nonfiction one, or the childrens one, or the graphic one, or the ones for ebooks and hardcovers and paperbacks. There's stuff for translated works too. Getting on any one of those only takes you selling out a very limited set of new york stores. You didn't exactly take off, you just happened to land in the right pocket of the right little market.

To make it worse that one shot is good for your whole career. The byline never says what year you pulled it off. Something you got away with in 2009 is still riding along on every thing you publish after that. Nobody is checking that you put it together since.

You end up in the store with that little name before your own, and the whole thing just stops having any bearing on how well the book in your hands actually sold. Every publisher is pushing it anyway so the label got so far out ahead of what it means that you can pretty much ignore it.

It's mostly a one time trick you get to advertise forever. You get on the list by pumping a big batch of copies into the exact stores the Times pulls its figures from in a given week. That little surge gets your name printed on that week's paper. From that point on the publishers put the line on the jacket of the next book. And the one after that. The claim is technically never out of date even though the feat behind it is. You've almost certainly never seen a book that wasn't once on that list, since almost every publisher will game the system at some point. You just never hear about the many narrow lists it's actually made up of. The whole thing ends up giving a false impression of some lasting public approval.

The lists also only catch the sales the Times can get a handle on. Your local independent or a direct order is going to be missed entirely. So the picture you end up with is of a fairly small and very particular collection of transactions that just happen to be highly visible.

It's mostly a matter of just how many separate lists they keep. You've got the regular fiction and non fiction ones but they throw in a whole lot of narrower segments on top. You've got a list for kids, one for mystery, one for regional interest and so on. Getting onto the regional ones can take surprisingly few sales because the total pool you are up against is so small. The moment you get your name down on one of these the publisher gets to use the exact same banner. That banner has to say nothing about which list you actually made. It gets slapped on every other title that person has put out no matter how different the subject matter is.

That basic trick gets multiplied out by agents who are happy to grab onto the most obscure qualification they can find. The whole thing ends up looking to a book buyer like a pretty broad success. They are taking a much smaller hit on the risk side of the ledger than the covers would lead them to think. You almost never have any easy way to figure out which of the many lists the rosy claim is actually pointing to.

Most of it is down to the list only looking at one week of sales. You can game that by getting a bunch of your best friends and family to go out and buy a copy right when the tally is taken. The publisher can do the same thing by getting a huge initial run into a tight group of stores. If you manage to get on that week's list the label gets added to the book's jacket and reprinted on every future edition. You are then selling a book that claims to have been enthusiastically purchased by the public at large.

It becomes a bit of a closed circle from that point. Nobody takes a hard look at how the sales were actually achieved since the label alone carries so much weight. You end up with a situation where the supposed measure of total public acclaim is really nothing more than a quick hit of locally arranged enthusiasm. You have only to look at the sheer volume of the label to see that something in the process has gotten badly out of hand.

You only need to make one of a bunch of different lists. There's fiction and non fiction, adult and children's, and a dozen other break outs. A book that hits the one week top ten in the Christian section can run the same headline as one that ran on the main literary list for a month. The wording they pick out never mentions which list you got on. You make the list for a short time, you get the blurb put on the cover, and then the blurb stays there. The lists get updated on different schedules too so you can duck into a gap in the schedule to get your claim on the record.

It gets reprinted on the jacket and then the whole thing gets copied over to the marketing copy that booksellers have to work with. Almost nobody goes back to see which particular list produced the result. You end up seeing the same by line on a whole lot of books that have nothing in common. It was a pretty useful little loophole for a while until almost every publisher figured it out.

It mostly works by a maximum number of titles per week. The whole thing is just a reflection of the total number of copies shipped out in a given stretch. Ship a big enough number to a bunch of different regional distributors and you get on the list. That covers everything from a major novel with a huge fan base to some very niche topic that a big chain happens to be pushing. Once you are on the list you get the right to slap that phrase on the cover and it tends to stick. You end up with a whole shelf of it since a book stays in print for years. You can get the little line based on a single week of heavy wholesale numbers way back.

It stops being a very useful thing to look at pretty much as soon as it gets used so much. You aren't getting any idea of how good something actually is. You are just looking at a record of who was able to get the most number of boxes to warehouses. It is just a sales figure dressed up as a stamp of approval and the sales part of the deal involves a whole lot of guess work on the part of the book sellers.

It's mostly a matter of how many lists they keep. The one you think of as the official list is actually a mashup of a dozen or so. You get the separate fiction and nonfiction ones for hardcovers and paperbacks, plus a long tail of narrower categories. There are lists for children, for the religious market, and for a bunch of other sub niches. Getting on any one of those is enough to put that label on the jacket. And once it's there it stays there. Nobody reprints with the claim scrubbed out.

That last bit is what does the heavy lifting. A book that shows up on some obscure regional or specialty list for a single week has earned a credential that looks to a casual shopper just like it had topped the main list. You then see that credential used to get the thing noticed by the people who put together the big combined list. Everybody involved is telling the truth but the whole thing adds up to nothing but the impression that every damn book on the shelf has been lionized.

It's mostly a matter of how many different lists they keep. You've got the hardcover fiction one, then the paper back one, and then a separate set for nonfiction, business, and religion. Add in the kids and the specialty ones and you get a pretty big menu. A publisher only has to get a title into the bottom third of any one of those lists for a single week. They don't have to have sold out the country.

Once you have that one week of placement the marketing people are finished doing the actual measuring. They just take the result and hammer it onto every future printing. You will see the same person get credit for placing on three or four of the lists in the bio section. Its a bit like someone who had a thirty second part on a small show claiming to have been seen on national television. You end up with the whole thing looking far more impressive than the raw numbers would suggest.

There's a fiction list, a nonfiction list, aChildrens list, a graphic list, a hardcover list, a paperback list, an ebooks list, plus lists for translated works and a bunch of genre-specific ones.
