texts: You can find 'em if you look in the right places. Dannon put out a bunch back in the late 90s, and a few smaller brands still make them. You just won't see them on the main shelves. You've got a couple of problems on your hands though. You can't color the thing without using some pretty obvious artificial dyes, since the real fruit gives you a nasty looking purple. Most folks will only buy a berry colored product if it looks red. That purple thing also has a flavor profile that comes across as pretty harsh. You end up needing a lot of it to get a taste you can stand, which隆隆 up the price. It stalls out in the testing phase because the sample folks don't rush to be first in line. Get a big enough group that would actually lap it up and you'd probably see the product get a second chance.

You've mostly got it. You tried a few times, mostly in the seventies, and universally got burned. The tannins in grape juice make your mouth pucker in a way that butts right up against the smooth texture you're after. Mix that with the pectin already in the juice and you end up with a result that sets out all wrong. You can't just steam it out either because that blows away the very flavor you were going for. You're left with either something that tastes like grape jelly on the nose of a sour milk flavor, or something so watered down it isn't really grape at all.

Kids do seem to like the stuff a lot more than adults do which is kind of interesting. But the people who develop the products mostly listen to the older crowd. So it never got to a second try. You've got the same dynamic play out in a few other fruit combinations. The thing is just more visible with grapes.

You can mostly blame the tannins. Red grapes are loaded with 'em, they're the same stuff that makes you pucker in a glass of red wine. You throw that conditional on top of the natural acid in the milk and you end up with a sort of muddy chalky mess. Blueberries got the same dark fruity note without that bite, so they took off. With green grapes you dodge the tannins but you end up with a thin watermelon like taste that nobody's asking for. You could bury that problem under a mountain of sugar and other things, but then there isn't much grape left to taste.

You probably won't see the same result if you go after the milk part of the equation. It's a common enough thought that the milk proteins are going to grab onto the tannins and ruin the flavor. That never really seems to be the case with cream either. You'd get the same messed up results in a frozen dessert. The tannin problem is something you can sidestep in a Jell-O since the gelatin has already sorted it out.

You've probably just been looking in the wrong places. Dale in St. Louis makes a pretty decent one and a bunch of the Greek brands have tinkered with it. You'll usually only find it in the fruit section of the big chains or at some of the smaller more out of the way shops. For most of the year here in the U.S it comes and goes. Nobody has the stomach to gamble on it in any size since the kids who are your real target will not run out to buy it. You end up with it getting swept off the shelves as soon as sales drop. You will not find it anywhere near as consistently as you would with the Cherry or the Lemon. That is fairly likely the reason you have come to the conclusion it does not exist.

You actually can get it in a few places and you can put the juice in the cup yourself. It just never made it to the end caps. The trouble is that grape has this one really sharp bite. You can get away with that in a soda because the carbonation drowns it out. You can't do that with yogurt. The dairy tang and the fruit tart kind of get in each other's way. You end up having to throw in a lot of sugar to get a pleasant result and that makes the thing taste like a gummy. It also comes out a really intense dark purple which seems to scare off people who are expecting a whitish base. You will see the two of them get along in a little better way in those cups with the fruit sitting in the bottom. Fully blended together the whole thing has just never found any sort of success.

You're mostly right, you just run into them less. You'll spot a few regional brands and the occasional national line like Stork. But the whole thing doesn't get the shelf space the other flavors do. That's mostly a numbers game. You need a product to sell in massive bulk to make the production run pay off, and grape never quite gets there.

You've probably got a taste thing working against it too. Grapes carry that tannic, almost winey astringency. You end up with a weird clash when you try to fold that into the mild, creamy base of a yoghurt. It never quite satisfies the people after a tart berry bite or the ones who just want something plain and sweet. You see the same thing keep grape out of a lot of the big breakfast cereal lines. It just never got the universal appeal to hit that next level.

You've probably just hit a weird hole in your local distribution. You can find it in the small plastic cups they put out for kids, and a couple of the regional brands have been known to put it out. Upstate, for example, has churned it out more than once. You are also likely bumping into a fairly strong and long standing habit on the part of the average buyer to grab the same peach or strawberry variety. That habit tends to keep the less popular choices from getting the shelf space needed to be very visible.

If you really want to track down a serving of it, your best bet is to fruit the line in the discount and convenience stores. Those places are far more likely to keep the less fashionable items in stock than a standard grocery shop. Quite a bit of the product you are looking for has already been made and sold, it is just that it was never quite enough to become a lasting mainstay.

There were and still are, you're just running into the aftermath of a pretty memorable fiasco. Dannon put a Grape variety on the market back in the mid nineties and the response was almost immediately and ferociously negative. The angry phone calls that followed were so specific and personal that the company decided to pull it. That combination of a very real consumer revolt and the resulting disappearance from shelves is why the flavor seems to have never existed. You can still turn up the thing in a few places, usually from smaller regional brands that aren't going to draw quite so much attention.

You've also got a little bit of actual food chemistry working against it. Grapes carry a fair amount of tannin, the same thing that gives red wine its slightly drying in the back of your mouth. That element gets carried right over into a fruit flavoring and can make a yogurt taste somewhat astringent. You don't run into that problem to nearly the same degree with strawberry or peach. You could get around it with a little extra tweaking but by then the whole exercise has started to run up against that clamor of old grievances.

groups.question: I just had a full length dream about an insignificant person from school I talked to maybe once. Why is this? It's been 12 years
texts:
Your brain doesn't sort memories by how important the people in them were. It sorts them by the tangled web of things they got attached to. You probably said one throwaway thing to this kid that got welded onto some other half forgotten thing. All that stuff has been sitting in storage, and last night a random thought you'd had squirmed into that old chain and set it off. The kid is just the part of the chain you happened to get a clear view of. You wouldn't get any of that if you were up and alert. While you are half out of it your brain will keep insisting it must have been a secret signal. It wasn't. It was just a circuit that got tripped.

It happens with the most trivial things and you usually can't pull the thread back out once your eyes are open. If you really pressed on it you might find that some song you heard this morning or some odd thing you saw on a walk was the thing that got it all going. You missed it while the rest of the thing was still there.

There isn't a reason so much as there is a mechanism. Your long term storage isn't sorted by how much somebody mattered to you. It's a mess of loose threads. You probably ran into something today that accidentally grabbed one of those threads and the whole dang cluster came up at night. The once conversation is sitting right next to the school, the year, and a bunch of other almost forgotten junk. Give the nightmare machine that to work with and it will happily invent a two hour plot. The dream ran long because the story it had started was internally consistent enough to keep going. You are also left with a stronger memory of the dream itself because you have nothing else to compare it to. If it had been someone you still talk to your brain would probably have glossed right over it.

You will not get any kind of hidden message out of it either. People read that in all the time and you would be a lot better off not to. You just got a random sample from the vast archive you have been accumulating for the last twelve years.

You probably stored more than you think you did. Your waking brain got around to filing that one conversation under "never going to be useful again" and locked the door on it. You've lost the conscious handle to get back in. Your sleeping brain doesn't use those same handles. It digs through the whole mess and can pop that old thing right back to the surface. You end up getting a fairly vivid narrative out of a shred of original data.

It also isn't really about that person. Your brain is just using the person as a ready made character in some other little scenario it's putting together. You're noticing the weird specificity of the dream and jumping to the conclusion that your subconscious must have some deep interest in this particular individual. In all likelihood that's not the case.

And 12 years isn't nearly as big a jump as it feels. That stuff is still in there. You just hit on it by accident. You'll probably have something like this again a year or two from now with some other forgotten face.

You probably had some random trigger that day. The smell of a particular food, a phrase someone used, the way a room was laid out. That thing lights up a whole tangled web of old associations in your head. Your old acquaintance is one of the nodes, and the dream machine just grabs him as an anchor to build a story around. You have no way to get the trigger back in the morning, so the whole thing looks like it came out of nowhere.

Twelve years helps in a slightly devious way. You've lost pretty much all the specific detail of that one conversation. All that is left is some kind of vague emotional shape the memory carried. Your sleeping brain is perfectly willing to invent a whole new scenario to fill that shape in. The fact that it played out as one long connected sequence is just that it got into a groove and kept going.

You almost certainly have several hundred other people of that same minor caliber lying around in the same state. On a different night the same mechanism would have landed on one of them. You only notice the ones it happened to choose.

You almost certainly got hooked on some tiny detail, a phrase they used, a little situation you were both in. Your sleeping brain has stopped keeping a really careful line between your current concerns and old random bits like that. It just shoehorned the person in to fit the little story of the day. You'd never get to them on purpose the way you do while awake, because waking memory sorts things by what is currently useful. The dream never cared that the person was in any real sense unimportant. It only cared that the stray bit happened to fit.

You could equally well guess that something else you were mulling over had just enough of a loose resemblance to pull the person in. You can't work backwards from the result to the cause. The machinery is too full of chance for that to come out as anything you can read off afterwards. You would have ended up somewhere different from any of a great many other possible starting points.

Your brain doesn't really have a good system for filing off the sort of encounter you're describing. You got the whole texture of that person in one go, voice and body and setting, and then it went into a storage bin with nothing attached to it. Since you never ran into them again you never got a chance to work the thing into a bigger story. That keeps the memory in something like its original state. It just needs some little random association to get it out and then your attention grabs hold. You are seeing a ten second clip and your brain fills in the other ninety. The whole movie is its own making. You never even knew the little clip was in there. That's mostly what you are getting.

That the thing has been sitting around for a dozen years mostly just makes it feel more uncanny. You have lost all count of the original event so it looks as though the dream has produced itself out of the blue. It hasn't. It has simply found the one copy that got saved and left there. You have simply forgotten that the copy was there all along. Nothing much need be made of it. It is a fairly ordinary bit of housekeeping that you happen to have caught in the act.

Your brain is basically a pattern matching machine that doesn't keep files sorted by importance to you. That one interaction got latched onto some feeling or sensory detail and it sat in there. You probably had some unrelated thing on your mind the night you slept and that random tag got snagged. The dreaming part of the brain then had to explain that snag and it made a little story around it. You get a full narrative out of what was essentially a half second of conversation. It's the same trick that lets you remember the exact words of a weird thing someone said while the rest of the class is gone.

The twelve years don't really change any of that. You are not accessing some kind of hidden significance. You are looking back and deciding the memory must have meant something when the truth is it was just one tiny hook the sleeping mind happened to pull on. You likely will never figure out what set that hook off that night.

Your brain doesn't keep a ledger of who mattered and who didn't. It encodes things by how weird or intense they felt in the moment. One slightly off conversation with this person probably got slotted in deeper than a hundred boring ones would have. From where your conscious mind sits, the encounter seems insignificant. Your storage system disagreed.

You're also almost certainly not getting a look back at the real person. The dreaming brain is a really loose thing, it grabs a face or a phrase and then merrily invents a whole plot around it. That person is basically a prop. You've probably done the same thing with a dozen other fragmentary bits you've picked up since. Pulling a thread from that one half remembered encounter was probably more or less random.

You've got twelve years in there too. That's plenty of time for the original memory to get edited out in a dozen ways. The version you saw in the dream is probably about as far from the actual encounter as you could get. You weren't really thinking of that kid to begin with. You were just using the bits you had left.

groups.question: What are the curving lines that appear in digital photos of computer screens?
texts:
You're looking at a moire pattern. Both the screen and the camera have a very regular grid. The screen is a tight checkerboard of red, green and blue subpixels while the camera's sensor is covered by its own repeating array of color filters. When you overlay two grids that aren't exactly the same size or angle you get that big sweeping interference, sort of like the shadows you get by holding up two window screens. That particular interference is what your eyes read as those curved bands. The bands end up looking rainbow because the three different subpixel colors interfere at slightly different scales.

You can get rid of it by changing the angle or the distance between you and the screen. Tilt the camera a bit and you'll almost certainly make the bands move or disappear. You run into the same thing in the real world, too, it's what makes the pattern on a herringbone suit look like it is constantly moving.

It's the same trick you get if you look at a picket fence through a window screen. Both the fence and the screen have a regular spacing and your eyes see a third and much coarser pattern where the two overlap. A camera sensor has an even tighter regular grid of red, green and blue light detectors, and the screen is doing the same thing. When you line them up the two grids beat against one another to produce those big sweeping bands. The bands change color because the two color layouts are slightly out of step, and they scroll if you move either the camera or the screen. You'll see the whole thing much more easily on an old tube since those had a really fine and unbroken phosphor grid to interfere with. Modern flat panels mess with the sensor enough that the whole thing fades in and out.

You're looking at a moiré. You've got two regular grids overlapping, the rows of pixels in the camera's sensor and the rows of pixels on the screen. When the two don't line up you get a new, much slower varying pattern on top. Get the angle between the grids even a little off and that slow pattern takes the shape of those big sweeping curves. Move the camera around and the curves will drift or change shape. On old tube TVs you were also seeing the screen's refresh cycle interfere with the camera's, which is what made the bands crawl. You'd get a fair bit of the same thing shooting a woven fabric, since the weave plays the same part the pixel grids do.

You'll get the same result with two bar codes laid nearly on top of each other. Put them at just the wrong angle and big loops pop out of the resulting overlap, and there's no magic to the effect beyond the two sets of lines getting in each other's way.

You're watching two separate time keeping mechanisms fail to agree. The monitor paints its picture from the top of the screen down, and the whole job takes a few milliseconds. Your camera nearly does the same thing with a rolling shutter. Neither one knows or cares about the other's schedule. So one part of the picture your camera ends up with was taken while the screen was showing one state, and another part was taken while the screen had already moved on. That little bit of phase difference gets your eye to read it as a sweeping band of color.

Move your phone around and you'll change the relative timing and see the bands jump around. If you slow the shutter speed down the effect gets worse and the bands get thicker. You actually get something of the same thing from photographing fluorescent lights, it's just a lot less rainbow. You'll pretty much never see the effect from a truly instantaneous exposure, though you'll almost never get that from the little gadgets you carry around.

They're a kind of interference pattern, and the technical name for the whole business is moire. You're effectively looking at the monitor's own grid of tiny pixels through the camera's grid of light sensing elements. The two grids are never quite the same size, and they are almost never lined up in a parallel fashion. groups.question: Why did TV and computer screens used to flicker in videos, and now they don't?
texts:
It's mostly a matter of how the thing gets painted on. The old cathode ray tube screens were a narrow beam of electrons sweeping across a glass face, top to bottom, over and over. Your brain sort of stitched those passes together into a steady picture for you. That trick only worked well up to a point, and in dim light the gaps between passes got easy to see. You ran into the same thing ever so often trying to film a tube with a camera that was tuned to a slightly different rate.

The new flat panels took a different shortcut. An LCD or an OLED keeps every one of its little pixels at a given brightness until the next whole frame is ready to swap in. Since there's no beam to sweep in the first place, there are no gaps for you to catch. You'll still notice things if the frame rate is low enough, but the problem it causes is different from the old scan line shimmer.

If you ever still catch what looks like flicker on a modern panel it is almost certainly the camera doing it. Cameras with fixed rates are far more prone to pick up a mismatch than your eyes are.

You're mostly seeing a math problem. In the US old monitors painted the whole picture 60 times a second, and the painting started from the top each time. A movie camera only grabs 24 of those snaps per second. So each one you get keeps catching the painter in a different vertical position. Play it back and you get a slow dark band rolling up the picture, and your eye tags that as flicker. Over in Europe the matching pair was 50 with 25 so the rolling band moved more slowly and got missed more of the time.

You stopped seeing it by changing one of those two numbers. Later video recorders took in fast enough to see a whole full set of repaints inside each of their frames. And displays for playing back movies got modes that matched the movie rate. The newest kinds of panels also just don't get redrawn in that top down manner in the first place. You are still stuck with the same pair of numbers, youve just made sure the two of them no longer get in each others way.

You are mostly remembering a mismatch between the content and the thing playing it. Movies get shot at 24 frames a second, and you were watching them on displays that repainted the picture 50 or 60 times every second. When two of those rates get layered on top of each other they make a visible serpentine or pulsing effect. The picture tubes you got all this from, being CRTs, made the light level vary in a way that let your eye pick off the problem. Putting the same film through a 120 hertz display would mostly patch up the arithmetic. Software doing a bit of frame duplication got there a little sooner.

You have run into some genuine flicker in the recordings as well though. Early video camera tubes and the low light levels available to them made that sort of thing fairly common. Once you got higher sensitivity sensors the毛病 all but disappeared. So you are fighting both the way the thing was recorded and the way it got played back.

You were mostly looking at a side effect of how cathode ray tubes made pictures. An electron beam swept across the glass in very thin lines and the phosphor it hit would light up then fade almost right away. You needed the beam to come back over and over just to keep the image from going dark. If that came back at a low enough speed the gaps in time got visible to your eye and that's what you called flicker. They got around it a bit by running the beam at higher speeds and also by painting one set of lines on one pass and the other set on the next.

None of that carries over to the flat panels we use now. The liquid crystals in an LCD or the cells in a plasma tube just stay in the state you put them in. You set a pixel to a certain color and it holds that color until you go back and change it. The frames still get replaced in a regular sequence but the old gaps never occur to begin with. That said some cheap inverter driven backlights still do a little bit of pulsing it's just way harder to spot.

It's two different refresh rates getting in each other's way. The old CRTs lit their picture up in a series of distinct sweeps, and a movie camera running at 24 frames a second would catch those sweeps at slightly different points. The result is that pulsing brightness and those rolling bands of light you've no doubt spotted in old films. You just weren't seeing the problem when you used the machines in front of them. Now you're mostly looking at LCD or OLED panels which keep an image on screen right up to the next one. That steady, unchanging glow just doesn't give the camera anything to clash with. You also get a lot of help from high speed capture and frame blending software that can mathematically iron the effect out.

That said you will still see it if you happen to film an old VFD or some other very fast refreshing device with a low end camera. You are just far less likely to run into one of these things these days.

You were looking at an electron beam that swept down the glass 50 or 60 times a second. In the tiny gap between one sweep and the next the picture went out, and that on and off is the flicker you saw. You mostly got used to it since your eyes fill in the gaps, but any camera with a different frame rate would catch it as a rolling band of light. Get a camera running at 120 frames a second and the thing becomes impossible to miss.

The panels you use now keep a fixed set of light sources on at all times. They just change the images being shown in front of that light. There is no dark gap in the display cycle for your eyes, or a camera, to catch. You do still get a smattering of the same sorts of problems out of the low end gear that fakes a dimmer setting by rapidly chopping that light. Most people are just used to ignoring it.

It's mostly a matter of what the thing you are looking at does to make a picture. The old vacuum tube sets, in both the living room and the office, had to paint an image on a phosphor coated glass. That painting happened in a fast top to bottom sweep, and your eyes were just good enough to clock the fact that they were looking at a half finished picture between sweeps. Interlacing things up only made that a bit more annoying. You were looking at 50 or 60 of these sweeps every second, right about where the brain starts to notice the gaps.

You killed that problem by throwing the vacuum tubes away. The flat panel stuff that replaced them simply has the whole picture on at once and then holds it there until the next one gets swapped in. You are still getting a new frame 60 or more times a second, but since every one of them is complete there is no visible drop out. You do still catch a little of it with really sensitive eyes in a darkened room, but it isn't a day to day annoyance in the way it once was.

You were watching a beam of electrons paint the picture over and over, one thin horizontal line at a time. The stuff on the inside of the tube glows when hit and then dies off pretty fast, so either the beam had to come back or the screen got dark. It came back every thirty or sixty of those thousandths of a second, and your eye managed to see the little dark part of that cycle. You'd catch the whole thing in spades if you pointed a cell phone at the thing. The phone's own frame rate gets out of step with the beam, and that mismatch is what showed up as that fast rolling bright band.

You got rid of it in two ways. The first was swapping the tube out for a bunch of little liquid crystal cells. Those keep an image on by holding a fixed voltage and don't depend on some fast re painting. The second was just cranking the speed of the re painting way up. At a hundred and forty four or two and forty times a second the dark part of the cycle is too brief to pick out anymore. You can still get a little of it if you are watching a cheap low speed set, but it isn't nearly as bad as it was.

groups.question: A couple days ago, a 300 year old Stradivarius violin was stolen (and later found.) What would be the point of stealing something so famous that anyone who can afford the million-dollar price tag would recognize as a stolen item?
texts:
It mostly isn't about getting the value out in the first place. You can't sell it to any serious player or to the few people rich enough to pay that sort of figure, because every one of them keeps a close eye on the lists. The same goes for auction houses and the handful of intermediaries who might be tempted to help. You end up with an object you can't play in public and that you can't safely put back into circulation.

Sometimes the play is to get someone who doesn't know better to take it in for you, and you keep peeling it through enough layers until the original taint wears off. That scheme works far less well than you'd hope. In the best case you end up making a small fraction of the price you were originally after. More often the whole thing鹦 works out to just getting you into a bit of legal trouble once the thing gets located.

You also get a certain amount of private pleasure out of having the thing to yourself for a spell. That has to be pretty much the only upside to the whole affair.

You'd never get the full million. That part you've already got. But you don't need to. The provenance trade is full of convincing enough fakes. You get a lawyer in a circle you trust to write up a totally made up history. Some purchaser with more faith in that story than in the official record ends up shelling out. You walk away with a fraction of the true value and that is still a very nice payday.

You have a second option as well. You know exactly who the thing belongs to. That person has every incentive to keep the whole mess quiet and pay you to get it back. The fact that the whole world would know it was stolen doesn't matter much in a private negotiation between you and the owner. You don't have to fence the thing to anyone else.

You are not out to get the market price. You are out to get some chunk of it by other means.

You aren't trying to sell it to someone who knows what it is. You're trying to unload it on someone who doesn't. That could be a collector in some backwater who's been told it's a fine Italian work from, say, the sixteenth century. He'll pay a maybe a tenth of the real value and you'll never see the rest. The instrument just gets tucked away in a private collection where no one with the references to check it will ever get a look at it. You're essentially gambling on how long it will take for the right pair of knowledgeable eyes to happen to fall on it.

There is also the option of simply holding it for a ransom. No third party gets mixed in and the whole thing comes down to how much the owners will pay to get it back. That tends to be a lot more than you could ever hope to get getting it off your hands. In either case you are guaranteed to take a whole lot of losses on the appraised value anyway.

You just need one buyer. You're not trying to get the thing to pass muster with the whole market. A single person in a position to insist it's all above board is enough. Some of those people live in places where you can't easily check provenance. That one sale gets the thing into a private collection, and the next time it shows up it's got a sufficiently plausible chain of ownership. You've got to go back through every one of the previous transactions to get at the original theft, and nobody is going to bother. That's the whole laundering scheme.

You could also just never sell the thing at all. Play it and keep it. That's probably a fair fraction of the cases, and it means the instrument never has to survive any kind of vetting. And then you've got the occasional thief who would appear to have no idea what they pulled off and is simply hoping to offload it somewhere that won't ask too many questions.

None of that would be a problem if you could fingerprint the instrument to the same degree you can a person. But you can't. The whole thing gets reset by a paper trail you've managed to fabricate.

You can't sell the thing to a serious buyer. Any collector in a position to drop a million on a violin is going to get a documented history, and the documented history is out there. The whole point of taking it has to be holding it as leverage. You ask for a ransom, the owner pays, you send the thing back. The notoriety you're worried about is actually the only thing that makes that sort of arrangement possible. Nobody is going to pay a huge sum to get back a violin they couldn't have identified. That ransom model is also how a lot of the other famous instruments that have gone missing in the past have been dealt with. You are even likely to get some kind of recovery reward on top of that.

Getting out of a deal like that is a different matter. You would need to run the thing through some kind of shivariate operation to get it on a clean paper trail. Any syndicate that would be willing to take a chance on that sort of thing is going to be looking for returns on an investment of that size. Given the risk on both sides it is rather unlikely that anyone would take the thing and try to pass it off as legitimate.

You're assuming the thief has to find a third party to sell to. They don't. The whole thing is a ransom scheme played out with a little more class than your standard mugging. The instrument is famous enough that the original owner is instantly identifiable, and the press will make sure of it. You end up writing a very large check to get it back, usually on the condition that you don't call the cops. If you did, the owner's own history with the thing would end up in the public record. You see this sort of thing with other high end art all the time. The thing gets photographed for the front page and the note explaining how to put the whole mess to bed arrives in the mail.

That said the exercise is far from sure to work. You've only got a very short window before the various interested parties get to the piece. In this case a convenient lead got the music back to the right hands pretty quickly. But you've still got a brief period when the risk of that happy ending was quite small.

You'd never sell it as a Strad to the final buyer. That person would almost certainly know the instrument. The whole thing runs through a chain of middlemen, usually in countries where nobody is going to check. You might break it down to the fingerboard, the scroll, the back board, and move those out separately. At that point you are just selling old pieces of wood. Any of those parts might eventually end up in a restoration shop where an actual violin maker recognizes them. That is very likely how the thing got found in the first place.

There are also a lot of very convincing forgeries of Strads in the world. That gives you a ready made story for where an instrument allegedly came from. The end buyer is told it was legally acquired from some obscure collection. Only a very small number of specialists would have enough knowledge to raise a red flag. The whole thing is betting that the chain of sale can be worked through faster than the recognition catches up. That bet just happened not to work out this time.

You aren't trying to get it to some rich collector off a newspaper ad. The whole scheme pretty much comes down to getting it back to the person who lost it. You send a very vague little note that says you have the thing and will return it for a sum of money. That person almost always ends up paying. From the outside that looks like a straight up ransom. You can also just arrange a quick hand to hand sale with a person you already have some kind of history with. They can keep a pile of cold cash around for such an occasion. In either case the fact that everybody is watching the case works in your favor. It ends up making that one necessary get together all the easier to pull off. Nobody has to go through any explanation to see what you are holding.

groups.question: The world can't agree on standard units of measurement for anything except time. H ow come?
texts:
The day and the year end up doing your work for you. You can't reasonably argue that the sun takes fourteen or fifteen hours to get back to the same spot. That forces a shared reference no matter what your local customs are. You can fiddle with the names, but you keep coming back to the same observed cycle. Nobody had to sit down and vote on what a noon was.

Length and weight never got that kind of natural anchor. You could define a foot in terms of a king's leg and get by perfectly well for local trade. The real cost of your private system only shows up when you have to deal with someone from far away. For a lot of groups that never happened, so there was no emergency forcing a change. The metric stuff kept getting punted out to some later date that never arrived.

You are seeing the same thing in money. The dollar won out through a mix of gunboat diplomacy and the work of armies of accountants. No one got there because the stars seemed to demand it. You just finally ran out of other ways to do business.

You can't really get around it with time. If I say "we'll meet in 20" and you guess minutes while I had hours in mind the whole thing falls apart. With lengths you can muddle through far more easily. Bring the thing you want to measure along and you can sort it out on the spot. Nobody has to commit to a common rod or broomstick in advance.

You also get it for free from the sky. The sun gives you a day and the moon gives you something like a month, and everyone on the planet gets exactly the same demonstration of these. A forearm length, the distance to some local landmark, or the width of a standard workbench is by definition different from place to place. That is a pretty deep well to get out of.

You did eventually get a lot of that baggage sorted through the metric system, but that was a political project that took ages. The time keeping side of things never had to wait for that kind of agreement to get anything done.

You've sort of got this backwards. We've got every length and mass sorted out in the meter and the kilogram. That whole thing lives in something called the SI system that nearly every country has signed up to. The trouble is that a few places have got it into their heads to keep running on the old stuff. The US and Liberia and a couple of others are the main hold outs. You sign a treaty about what the units are supposed to be and that changes very little of what people actually do day to day.

Time is a different animal mostly because we got so much better at keeping it. You can now peg the length of a second to the way a cesium atom wiggles and have a lab in Osaka get the same result as one in London. That degree of exactness was never much of a selling point for measuring off a field or weighing a sack of grain. People were happy to let their foot stand in for a unit of length. Once a whole country builds up a stock of ships and bridges to match the old way of things the price of changing gets pretty steep. Nobody was going to pay that.

You've mostly got it backwards. You can get a Coke in liters or ounces and nobody gets too worked up about the difference. The whole of science, medicine and most of the manufacturing world runs on the metric system. You and the rest of the US are just the biggest bunch of holdouts. The rest of the non compliance is mostly down to old local traditions that nobody has been strong enough to override.

Time is just a different animal. It is tied to the sundial and the equinox in a way that you can't vote to change. Try to make the day ten hours long and you have got to force the sun to keep your schedule for you. The old lunisolar calendars got so hopelessly muddled with all their corrections that a clean numerical system was the only way to get out. You could see the advantage of that. With a ruler there was no mathematical dead end quite so convincing to drag in every old local custom.

You're in a bit of a hampered position here since the US is doing a lot of the not agreeing on your behalf. Almost everyone else, like the UK and Australia, swapped over to the metric system in the last century or so. You end up with the appearance of a global fight where really it's mostly you and a few other holdouts refusing to budge.

Time gets away with it because you can't easily get rid of the earth's rotation. You get your handy universal reference for free which is why twelve or twenty four hours worked out for so many different peoples. You don't get that same easily available standard for the length of a cubit or the weight of a bushel. Those were always local things and getting people to give up their own familiar measures proved to be a very sticky business.

You got that part mostly right. We all end up on the same page for time because the sun did the work for us. You split the time it takes to get around into 24 bits and you have a day that looks pretty much the same in every part of the globe. No committee had to get together to work it out. The practical daily use of the thing forced the issue.

Get a group of people together to agree on what a foot or an inch should be and you are in for a fight. Every little kingdom and guild had a vested interest in its own particular version. That sort of arrangement is very hard to shake off. You only got a bit of a global feel for that stuff in the last few hundred years with the metric system. Even that has run up against some pretty stubborn resistance. I still see a few folks in the US hanging on to the old way.

You've mostly got it backwards. We do have one set of standards out there for length and mass. The meter and the kilog are in use anywhere you'd go so long as you were doing any sort of technical work. The US is the main party that keeps hoggling along on a parallel system of feet and pounds. It ends up looking like a total lack of agreement even though the alternate system has pretty much been settled on. Time is the only case where the old local varieties got kicked out altogether. You might be able to muddle along with two different ideas of a foot, you simply can't get anywhere on a ship or run a factory if the days aren't the same length.

That said you wouldn't get much further with the old systems if you tried to force them into a decimal footing. A great number of the ratios you have come to rely upon just stop working out. The whole mess ends up keeping itself in being because the cost to switch is far too high for the very small amount you stand to gain.

You mostly get time for free off the earth. The day and the year are the same for a guy in Tokyo as they are for one in Omaha, since both are just watching the same rock go around the same star. You can't get that same natural fix for length or weight. Your average medieval foot differs from my average medieval foot because we've got different sized toes. That starts out as a small local variation and afterwards gets so thoroughly baked into the local economy that nobody can get people to agree otherwise.

You actually have got a pretty good deal on everything else these days too. The inch you use is now a fixed multiple of the centimeter, and the pound is pegged to the kilogram the same way. You just kept the old labels around. That's mostly the fault of the United States, which never got around to forcing the old ways out. Get that one holdout to budge and you wind up with a pretty thoroughly unified scheme.

groups.question: why is my school so sensitive to religion amongst students, but also purposely doesn't serve meat on Fridays?
texts:
You're not actually seeing two different standards. You're seeing one closed system that just happens to conceal some of its methods. The school is free to impose the stricter moral rules on your conduct because that conduct is part of the arrangement you agreed to by showing up. You don't get to veto that portion. The meat thing works the same way, only it has been dressed up to seem like a matter of habit or tradition. You squirm over both, but the arrangement that compels you to put up with one also compels you to put up with the other.

Pick and choose your objections and you'd soon find that the whole thing falls apart. That is quite obviously something the people running the place wanted to avoid. They aren't trying to be fair or consistent in any sense you are used to, they are merely enforcing a set of ideas they have agreed to accept as the final word. You dont have much recourse against that.

You're looking at the ido of a bunch of old papal laws. way back, every catholic had to give up meat on fridays. the school wasn't trying to make some kind of religious rule out of it, it was just trying to keep the kids from coming to class starved. you've got this whole generation of parents who weren't going to let their kids break that home habit. so the kettles simply got round to it. at the same time the place kept up the pretence of being perfectly neutral on religious matters otherwise. you've got to take the two things as a single practical arrangement that just never got cleaned out. you'd get much the same result if the custom had been to wear a particularly peculiar sort of dress.

you probably won't get the people in charge of the whole thing to explain it to you in just those terms though. the thing has got so much importance in the local way of thinking that actually putting a name to it would be more of a bother than is worth.

You are running into the difference between an institution's own identity and the rules that keep it from imposing that identity on everyone. That Friday meat ban is almost certainly a holdover from the school being founded by a Catholic order. Because that order wrote the mission statement the school operates under, the rules attached to it have just been handed down to the whole place. The law lets them keep that kind of in house tradition. What it won't let them get away with is taking a stand on what the students themselves have to believe. If they tried to push Catholic doctrine on the kids, or blocked out some other faith, they would get in serious legal trouble.

So the two things you are seeing aren't actually at odds with each other. The school is keeping its own distinct character while keeping its hands off the question of what the kids individually might hold. You would probably see the same setup at a bunch of other old religious schools that have to stay in that narrow legal lane.

You're probably looking at a habit the place picked up way back when. If it was ever run by monks or nuns they'd have kept to that old fast that keeps meat off the table every Friday. They kept the menu going long after the religious order had any real say in things. It is a lot less trouble to leave a long standing schedule alone than to go in and shake it up. You aren't seeing any real push for that custom either. The no religion rule is about what they put in their own classes and activities. You aren't really promoting a belief by getting up in the morning and eating beans. You could ask the administration to find out the exact year they first made the change. You'd probably find it lines up with some moment when the original founders got out.

You are mostly seeing a fossil. The Friday thing dates back to when the whole student body (or the people who run the place) was Catholic or maybe Orthodox. Nobody is out there telling you to observe a fast, they have just never gotten around to changing the menu. It is way easier to keep doing an old thing than to get a whole bunch of parents to agree on a new one. If you went and put a beef dinner on the menu tomorrow you'd get a lot of complaints from that old guard.

The rules you are getting from the administration are the opposite of that. They are only as strict as the courts have forced them to be. You have to avoid stepping on any group's toes in the first place so you cannot end up taking sides. You can't advertise the Friday fish as a religious thing but you also can't bring yourself to scrap a habit that has been around for decades. You got the strictest part of the modern rules and the laziest part of the old ones, and that combination is what looks like a double standard to you.

It's mostly two different rulebooks getting in each others way. The Friday thing is almost certainly a hangover from when the school was run by a Catholic order. They never got around to changing the menu, and nobody felt like making a fuss about it. That kind of old routine gets left in place the way you'd leave an old family crest on a new building. It isn't anybody's religion at that point. It's just the way the place has always done things.

The downside you are seeing on the student side comes from a whole different set of legal pressures. Once a school opens its doors to everybody, it gets a lot of heat for appearing to give any one group the inside track. Allowing a bunch of different folks to push their own stuff around tends to get you into fights you can't get out of. So the safe move is to put a pretty hard stop on that kind of thing.

You end up with the old stuff being allowed to coast along while the new stuff gets shut down. Neither of those decisions has much to do with the other. That said knowing a little more about what you have actually seen would help you sort out whether that is in fact the whole story. You might have some other local arrangement going on that I have no way of guessing at.

You are seeing two ends of the same rule. The first part has to do with the state not being seen to pick a side. You can't have teachers lead a prayer in class or put up a cross on the wall. That would be the state itself taking a position. The whole Friday thing gets away with it because it has ossified into something you might call a standing menu habit. It was a rule everybody used to follow and now nobody has a problem with it. Those who want to keep it up will just say it keeps the cost of the lunch program down.

Things would probably be a lot more straightforward at a private school. Those are free to plug a lot of their own values into the daily routine. The place you go to has to keep a fairly broad mix of kids from running afoul of one another. Both of the practices you have in mind are really just two different ways of getting that done.

You are probably running into the difference between something you could get in trouble for and something you just take for granted. The no religion rule you see is pretty much straight out of the courts, which have made it illegal for public schools to endorse any faith. You get in trouble for saying happy Christmas in an official school capacity, for instance. That friday meatless meal never got hit by the same legal scrutiny. It just got stamped with the label of an old timey tradition that wasn't meant to proselytize. To the people running the place the two things aren't in the least bit contradictory. They have been told one thing is a religious endorsement and the other is simply how things have always been done.

You are not going to get a very straight answer by asking about the logic of it. If you want to be sure you are reading the history right you would have to get hold of the school's original founding documents. Those will probably spell out just how much of that whole friday thing was in the first place a way to practice the faith.

groups.question: when commercials say "Next 20 callers will receive..." How do they keep track of that?
texts:
It's mostly just a plain old counter in the phone system. You get a little patch of phone numbers and you plug in an auto attendant that keeps a running total. It plays the real pitch out loud to the people who get in, and once that total is up it switches over to a canned "that's too bad the offer just closed" thing. All the phones in the group look at that same number so they can't be gamed by redialing on the side lines.

You've also got that part where the caller has to repeat some numbers back to them. Those aren't there to prove that you live in the right area so much as to prove that a person actually read off the fine print. If they got the code right the little computer grinds away at the next bit of paperwork. It definitely feels like more of a magic trick than it is since every one of the 20 people gets a completely different set of numbers to recite.

You're mostly getting away with it. They've got a big board in the monitoring room that lists every call in the order it hits the line. Each one has a big time stamp on it and the guys watching that board just mark out the first 20 in the right window. If you're the 21st one to hit that list you get the polite "too late" spiel. The only wrinkle is that if the 20th person is deep in a conversation they'll let them finish.

You'd notice that they use the exact same setup for the free trial offers they tack onto the deal. The system doesn't really care what the specific deal is. It just sees a bunch of calls piling up in some order. The people watching it decide at what point to tell each caller they've made the cut. The whole thing is way more of a human gimmick than a technical feat.

There's a counter on the back end of the number. You'll know it from call center operations, it's the same stuff they use to report how many calls they're getting. First 20 hits the counter, everyone after that gets a different recorded message. They conditional on a zip code or area code too if the deal is supposed to be local.

That said a lot of it is theater. If you press the wrong key, or if the system is already overloaded, you'll get the "we've already filled up" version whether or not you really were 21st. You have no way of verifying the count from your end. Nobody's keeping a public list.

You'd get a lot of the same effect with a bunch of little routing rules, and adding up a bunch of calls in different groups. The math gets pretty ugly to check from the outside. So they do whatever is easiest to implement and call it an honest count.

It's basically a dumb counter. The free code gets routed to a computer running some pretty rough software. That software just keeps a tally of how many calls have come in. You hit twenty and it stops sending you to the prize giving circuit and plays back a "sorry you're too late" recording from that point on. You generally aren't even identified as an individual, it's just a matter of getting through the line in time. That last part is of course how the whole thing got so full of abuse. People with a few phone lines could easily beat you to it.

They've got newer variations of the trick online with the 976 and 900 number schemes. Same fundamental setup, the only difference is the computer keeping the count now does so in a web environment. You'll find the same thing is going on with almost all those "first so many people get something" deals. They aren't really doing any individual vetting.

The phone company (or whatever call routing service they use) just gives them the first twenty numbers that come in. The promoters keep a little stop list of those. You can kind of hear it happening, the operator will read off a name from that list, say the offer is yours, and move on. Once the list is exhausted they start reading off the next pitch. Callers who happen to get a number on that first list have won, and everyone else gets the standard offer.

You'll occasionally see a more digital version where the system checks the incoming number against a database in real time. But you'd be very hard pressed to find an operation that does any of that for a cheap radio spot. The stop list approach is cheap enough and works well enough for the purpose. You do have to trust that the routing service will deliver the calls in the actual order they come in though.

They've got a call tracking box in front of the 800 number that just counts every call it gets. The box is set to stop counting after 20 and to feed you a different recorded message once it hits that number. Pretty much every call after that gets the "we're sorry, the promotion has ended" spiel. You've got common sense protections in place like asking for the order number of the item you were calling in for, that keep a person from calling back twice and taking two of the prizes.

You also hit a timing quirk the spots never get into. The first 20 people to get through to a live operator at some set time after the spot comes on are the ones who win. Your call a few seconds after the commercial is no good if the line isn't staffed yet. A lot of the earlier calls that get in get shunted to a holding message while they get sorted, so the whole thing ends up pretty much a lottery anyway.

It's mostly just a dumb part of the phone system. They throw enough circuits to take a fixed number of calls and once those are filled up the rest get a recorded message. The operators on those lines are usually counting along on some notepad too. So the first twenty to get through are the first twenty. They're not rerouting you or doing any sort of clever matching in the back. You'd see the same thing with a bunch of people calling into a radio game.

The whole thing only starts to look more complicated if a lot of people try to game it. You'll sometimes see them throw in some voice check just to make sure one person isn't run a whole party. That's about the limit of the sophistication you are going to get out of the operation though.

It's mostly a dumb counter sitting in front of the switchboard. All the lines get fed into a single auto attendant and that's where the counting happens. Every call that the system answers bumps the number up. When you hit 20 the thing just plays a "too late" message and stops passing calls through to the live show. You get a log of the whole thing kept just in case some sore loser calls back to argue. You can't stick a counter on each individual line though, that would give you 20 winners for every line you had.

It does depend a bit on what you're counting. You might only give out the prize for a call that actually gets through to a person, or you might count every single call the machine answers. And if someone wins and then can't be reached or turns out to be ineligible you have to either claw that count back or burn one of your 20 for nothing. Neither of those situations is all that hard to deal with, they just eat into the numbers you were planning on.

groups.question: What is the use of a birth certificate?
texts:
It's mostly a matter of getting anything else. You can't sign up for a driver's license, a passport or even get married without it. Banks are going to make you produce one too, and so are a lot of employers. Since it's the very first link in your whole chain of identification no other record is going to take its place. Losing one gets you stuck in a pretty expensive and slow process to get a certified copy from the state you were born in. You will have to go through that again and again for the rest of your life.

There are a few minor extras like being able to prove your age at a bar or in a court of law. But those all just fall out of the fact that no one will get you a license or a vote without that first document.

You can't get very far without one. You need it to get a driver's license, a passport, or a marriage license. Banks won't open an account for you and neither will most employers. It also gets you on the voter list in all but a couple of states. You'll find that pretty much every other official paper they ask you for gets checked against that first one. It is the only thing the government will take as a given that you are really the person you claim to be.

You can get a replacement copy if you manage to lose the original. The place you go for that is almost always the same state or territory where the first one was issued. A lost document will cost you a little money and some time, but it isn't the end of the matter.

It's the whole foundation your legal identity gets built on. You can't get a driver's license, a passport, or a marriage license without one. Banks won't open an account for you and you won't be able to vote. You'll need it to rent a car, check into a hotel, or get in to a bar. If you lose it every one of those other papers is basically useless since they all traced back to it. You do have to go through your state's vital records office to get a replacement and if you've changed your name and not gotten that change recorded you can get locked out of a lot of it.

You end up seeing the same thing in most other countries though the particular offices you have to deal with will be different. The pattern is the same everywhere since some central list has to exist that everyone else can refer to. That list is what the document certifies your place on.

It's the whole thing your other ID leans on. You can't get a driver's license or a passport without first showing one. Same goes for getting married or opening a bank account. Doctors will want to see it if you end up in the hospital, and you can't legally sign a long term contract on anything but that. It's the record that proves you are you to the outside world. If you lose it you can get a fresh copy from the office that keeps the original register, so getting rid of one doesn't actually get rid of the fact it certifies.

You might find you need one for less dramatic stuff too though. Getting your name back to what it used to be is pretty much impossible without getting it into the picture first.

It's the whole game in the end. You can't get a driver's license, a marriage license, or a passport without one and that pretty much gates you out of the rest of life. You'll hit it again when you try to get into the military or set up a bank account. The military is especially strict about the dates and spelling on it. It also serves as the thing you have to show to prove you are old enough to drink or buy a lottery ticket.

Since it isn't really the document you carry around the most you end up losing track of it a lot. The fix is to go back to the vital records office for the place you were born and get out a fresh certified copy. That office has the only original on file so you can't get around them. If you were born in a different state than the one you are living in now you will probably have to mail in your request.

It's the top of a pretty long list. You can't get a driver's license, a passport, or a marriage license without it. Banks will not open an account for you, and you'll hit the same wall when you try to take out a mortgage. Almost every job that requires a background check ends up asking for one. It is effectively the paper every other form of ID gets checked against. You sort of have a few work arounds like a military card or a tribal ID, but they only get you so far. Getting a court to declare your identity is another option, though that is a long and annoying business. You will end up needing the thing in the end anyway.

It's mostly a matter of getting anything else. You can't get a driver's license, a passport, or a marriage license in the US without one. Banks and employers will also want to see it to get your name and date of birth on the record. It doubles as the official record of who your parents are, which matters for things like inheritance. If you lost it and tried to get a replacement you'd find yourself stuck in a loop since that replacement would also depend on the original. Most other countries work out the same way, they just put a slightly different list of things behind that same first document. You make the trouble of proving your own existence one time and the rest of your life gets a lot easier.

It's the document everything else gets built on. You need it to get a driver's license, a passport, or a marriage license. Your local election office will want to see it before you can sign a voter registration. Banks and other lenders generally want a copy on file before they'll put a loan in your name. Hospitals will ask for it when you're admitted. If you ever lose a license or passport, you have to come back to the birth certificate to get a replacement. Without one you'd be stuck, since pretty much every other piece of official ID traces back to it.

It doesn't prove much by itself in a foreign country, and adoption papers or a naturalization certificate will supersede it in a few specific cases. But within your own country it's pretty much the only thing that gets you into the system in the first place.

groups.question: How did the commonality of "seeing the light" originate when people are "crossing over" or passing away?
texts: You've got pretty old precedents for it. Plato puts a returning dead man in the middle of the underworld in the fifth century BCE and has him describe two great paths, one leading to a place of great joy. You get the same fork in the road with the bright and the obscure route running through tons of medieval visions. The Tibetan Book of the Dead has the consciousness of the dying confronted with a glorious radiance it must choose to accept. What changed in the last half century is that people started to systematically round up first person reports from patients who had been clinically dead. Raymond Moody did this to very good effect in a widely read book in the seventies. He made the radiance seem like a regular thing that just happens to everyone. Once you line up a batch of testimonials that all mention the same thing you get a lot of folk ready to take their word for it. The stories are also so handy for preaching the need to pick the right side that they just kept getting repeated. You don't have to believe any of it was supernatural to get it passed off that way.

You're mostly talking about the stuff people report after getting resuscitated, since nobody who has fully gone can get back to describe it. On the medical side the temporal lobe is a fair suspect, it gets all sorts of haywire electrical activity when you're starved of oxygen. The visual cortex will throw off a bright white flash under those same conditions, not that different from you seeing one after a bad head bump. You also get a tunneling of your vision as things get worse, which conveniently frames that flash as a light at the end of a tunnel.

None of that gets you the tunnel of falling dead people or the other narrative bits though. And the fact that you get "light" reports from folks who had no religious expectation of one pretty much kills the idea that it's all in their heads. You end up with a mess of partial answers that none of them quite cover the whole thing. It's one of those questions where the honest reply is still that no one has figured out what's actually going on.

You've got a fair handful of explanations bouncing around and none of them quite splits cleanly from the others. The tunnel part is probably your visual cortex doing a bit of show. When blood flow to the brain gets interrupted the outer portions of your vision go first and what's left looks like a passage. Get the edges right and a bright center pretty much takes care of itself. The Chinese team that played with electrical stimulation got a pretty clear demonstration of that bit. The more personal and numinous elements seem to come from the temporal lobe, the part your brain uses to build a sense of self. Poke that with electricity and people report encountering beings of unusual significance.

You can't drop the cultural piece out of the picture either. The whole thing gets slotted into the vocabulary people already know to be true and that is what gets reported back. You get pretty much the same basic neurological event wearing out a different set of clothes depending on which tradition the person happens to be born into. You can pick out a piece of the mechanism for almost every aspect of the story. You just can't yet get a single one to account for the whole thing.

You've got a lot of testimony to work with and it comes out pretty much the same in a bunch of different countries. That's the part that gets people thinking some shared mechanism is at work. The usual neurological answer is that a brain starved of oxygen starts dumping off random signals in the temporal lobe. Your mind then stitches those signals together into something it can make sense of, and a passageway with light at the end is one of the results you keep getting. You can reproduce a fair bit of that with epilepsy or by zapping the lobe with electricity. The other thing you have to count on is that people have been told over and over what to expect. So they end up reporting what they already had in mind as an explanation.

You can't really sort those two things out from the outside. The same feeling of a passage toward a bright light turns out to be producible by either a brain in trouble or a very well prepared expectation. Whether either of those gets at the real cause is something the evidence so far hasn't gotten to the bottom of.

You're mostly picking up the idiom from the fact that so many people from completely different backgrounds report the same basic thing. It's a bright light they are moving toward, and it's what they tend to take for some kind of afterlife. You get the same story out of a满眼 of Christians as you do from Hindus, though the two will furnish it with very different details. That does not prove there is some universal spiritual truth in play, it just means the brains of all those people are getting jammed in the same way. When the temporal lobe fires oddly you end up with very convincing sensations that your mind then explains through what it already knows. A Christian is going to read it as an entry into heaven, a Muslim will read it very differently. The light apparently comes from the malfunction and the meaning you attach to it comes from your own background.

You also have to keep in mind that all of this is built on testimony you can't check. You can't exactly rig up the recording gear to watch it happen, and the people being asked about it have usually already lost a lot of their grip on what actually transpired. Nobody has actually pinned down a single reliable mechanism, and the whole business is bound to remain pretty speculative.

You're mostly looking at two things that happen to line up. A lot of the sensory part has a pretty clear physiological root. When the heart stops or blood flow to the head drops, the outer part of your visual field goes dark first. That leaves a narrowing circle you experience as a tunnel. Your brain, starved of what it expects, tends to fill that central point with a bright sensation. You've got a tunnel and a light at the end without anyone being able to point to a source. Doctors have gotten something similar out of people by zapping specific regions of the temporal lobe.

The "going to the other side" story is a separate layer people build on top of that raw sensation. You get the tunnel and light, then your own set of cultural ideas tells you what it means. The fact that you hear this story in so many different places just suggests that the underlying brain event is very much the same everywhere. The tunnel is what your failing vision makes of it.

As for the phrase you're asking about, that's just an old way of talking about the end. Darkness and the putting out of lamps was an early set of images, and inverting them to describe a destination was an easy step. We've been doing that for a very long time.

You've got a few things braided together. Up through the 18th century the whole religious baggage in Europe had a very fixed idea of heaven. The book of revelation has that city you don't need a sun for, made of jasper and filled with this uncreated radiance. You saw it everywhere in the pictures of the saints with their little circles of blaze around their heads. The stories people told each other had that light in them already. Then you start getting a steady drumbeat of 19th and 20th century accounts from people who had had near death experiences. They kept on mentioning a bright light at the end of a tunnel. That got written into the popular record and then looped back to color the next round of reports.

The tunnel part you can probably chalk up to your own eyes. Once your blood flow to the brain starts to drop your visual field constricts in on itself, and that tends to leave you with a central bright spot. You are describing a purely mechanical effect in words you learned from somewhere. You end up telling a religious story about it because that is the only shape the story had for you. It is probably impossible to tell from the outside whether those early reports set the pattern or whether the pattern simply sorted itself out to match them.

You are actually running two separate things together and it is your own mind that stitches them back together. The tunnel part has a pretty dry explanation. Your optic nerve has a blind spot and the whole visual field is sort of tubular on the outskirts. When blood flow to the brain drops off, the central vision gets pinched out first, leaving a shrinking ring of sight. If that ring happens to include a bright light the whole thing looks like a glowing passage. You can get the same effect from various drugs and from animal hypnosis, which suggests no special agency is required.

The whole glowing passage business has been baked into the afterlife imaginings of the Jewish and Christian traditions for a very long time. Once you have an experience that is so emotionally intense your brain is going to try to file it away under the most familiar headings it has. For a lot of people those headings were already set. You obviously never hear the equivalents of the old fellow who crossed over and found himself in a rather unhelpful parking lot.

The thing to keep in mind is that there is not some single plot running behind it. You have the cold mechanics of the failing eye on one hand and a very well worn set of stories on the other. The two end up perfectly matched in the retelling.
