groups.question: What is the speed of electricity?
texts:
You're really asking about two different things. The signal that tells your light to come on gets along at something like two thirds to nine tenths of the speed of light. What that is depends on what your wires are made of. The electrons themselves are awful slow in that same copper. You might catch them managing a fraction of a millimeter in a second. You get your light almost at once because that first group of electrons shoves the next one along the whole length of the wire. It works exactly like a very long line of marbles.

You will get some other numbers if you look at the radio waves the power meter uses to get a reading back to the company. Those would in fact go at the full speed of light in open air. None of what I've been saying changes the fact that the little bit of energy you actually use to get any job done takes its time getting there.

You're almost certainly thinking of the signal, which moves down the wire at a big fraction of the speed of light. You get somewhere between 50 and 99 percent of that 186,000 miles per second, and the difference just depends on what the wire is wrapped in. That is the part that makes a light come on the instant you close a switch. The individual electrons inside the metal are a different story, they inch along at a fraction of a millimeter per second. Throw a switch and you set up a push in the field around the wire, and that push is what races down the line.

You would see a sensible in between figure only if you started trying to pin down exactly how the energy gets from one end to the other. Except that you'd end up describing it as the field moving along at the wave speed anyway. The electrons you are picturing chugging through the metal are really just along for the ride.

It depends on what you are keeping your eye on. The signal that actually gets your light to turn on rides on an electromagnetic field and it gets there at something like 60 to 90 percent of the speed of light. That is fast enough that for any wiring you are likely to run around the house you would never see a time lag.

The electrons themselves are another matter. They are crowded together in the copper and they end up edging along at a few millimeters per second. You get the sense of something fast moving instantly because the push gets passed along that much more quickly. It is a bit like a long line of cars where the last guy starts to move before the first one has gone very far.

It's mostly the speed of light with a little left on the table. The signal that your switch sends out races down the wire at roughly 50 to 90 percent of that 186,000 miles per second. You end up with the lower number because of the plastic or rubber insulation wrapped around the inside. The free electrons moving along in that wire are getting along at quite a different clip. You might see an inch or two of them in the time it takes you to blink. So you get the light almost instantly even though the actual electrons that delivered it took forever to get there.

You will get different numbers if you're dealing with an open circuit or a transformer. In those cases the field just takes off at the full speed of light. The wire is more like a rail to keep the thing on a straight and narrow path.

Most of it is just the electromagnetic field getting along the wire and that one moves at a good chunk of light speed. You'll get maybe two thirds of that in a typical copper cable because the plastic insulation around it slows the field a bit. You get closer to the full 186,000 miles a second if that field has to move through air or a vacuum. The actual electrons in the copper are a separate story and they inch along at something like a few millimeters per second. It kind of works like a long pipe that is already filled with water since you get a result at the far end almost right away even though any one particular bit of water is moving very slowly.

You can't quite say what the speed is without saying something about the line you are using. The physics is the same but that insulating material is going to set the actual pace for the signal.

You've got two different things going on. The signal that tells the electrons what to do races down the wire at somewhere between 50 and 90 percent of the speed of light. That part is mostly a property of the insulating material you've wrapped around the conductor. The electrons themselves are an entirely different story and they end up shuffling along at a fraction of a millimeter per second. It's a bit like the way you can get a very strong push down a long water filled pipe almost instantly even though the individual water molecules take a long time to get there. You get the same near instantaneous result in a circuit for very much the same reason.

It doesn't really matter that the electrons are moving so slowly. The effect of applying a voltage propagates through the whole bunch of them at that very high speed. That is why a light bulb at the end of a long wire comes on the instant you flip the switch. Had the electrons had to crawl all the way there from the switch it would have taken an absurd amount of time.

It depends on what you've got in mind. The electrons themselves only get along at a tiny fraction of a millimeter a second. You wouldn't see that part at all if you were watching a light switch. What you are actually seeing is a signal zip down the line at a pretty good fraction of the speed of light. You can get as much as ninety percent of that top end with coaxial cable. Plain old copper wiring in a house will usually manage to get you about two thirds there.

That signal speed gets knocked around a bit by whatever they wrapped the conductor in to keep you from getting shocked. The more the insulation slows that signal down the more delay you end up with. In a house you will never notice a second of that delay. It becomes a fairly glaring issue once you get to the point of sending data around the globe.

It's two different things. The signal that you actually get to use, which is an electromagnetic wave running down the outside of the wire, gets along at roughly two thirds of the speed of light. Change the materials you use for the wire or its insulating covering and you change that fraction a bit. The electrons themselves are only getting pushed a tiny distance in that same time, crawling along at a pace of a few millimeters a second. You end up with the light in the other room almost at once because the push got there fast, not because any of the original electrons made the trip.

If you are talking about high voltage DC lines the situation is a bit more complicated since you get traveling surges to contend with. But for the vast majority of day to day applications the picture above pretty well describes what you are seeing.

groups.question: Why are death row inmates housed separately?
texts:
It's mostly a mix of protection for the inmate and the rest of the prison. You've got a pretty strong incentive for other guys to get even, and you can't really stop that unless you keep the target out of the general population. The same goes for stop the inmate from trying to get out. Trying to do that would just start another set of legal proceedings on top of the ones you already have.

It also comes down to the fact that the appeals process ends up taking decades. That makes a "temporary" arrangement the only way to do it. You end up with a whole lot of long term isolation that you might not have been too隆隆 worried about when you first set the rules. Almost every state handles the little details of that a little differently anyway.

You mostly can't put them in the general population. Someone in there is going to try to kill you in retaliation for what you did, and that's hard to prevent. Same problem runs the other way, you don't want people getting information to skip out on a transport. Keeping a tight group in one place also makes it easier to run the long legal process out in front of an actual execution. You've got to get the whole thing set up and that's almost impossible to do with a person split up through the rest of the place.

You do end up with a lot of psychological harm as a result though. Most of that time is spent in a small locked cell with very little in the way of outside contact. That just seems to happen because there isn't much of an alternative. It isn't really the point to torture anyone, the whole thing is just the by product of trying to keep everyone from dying in some other way.

It's mostly because of the security headaches they create. You've got people who might try to kill a guard or get out, and then you have the very real risk that other prisoners will try to get even. Stuffing them in the general population makes both of those odds go up. You need a lot more staff eyes on them, and that's just easier to do in a specific wing.

Then there is the legal side. They are entitled to prepare appeals and that takes a ton of time and paperwork. Trying to get that done in a regular cell block is a nightmare. Concentrating them in one place makes shuffling legal materials around a lot more straightforward. You also end up with a situation where the isolation and tight rules act as a sort of extra punishment. That never shows up in the official reasoning but it is pretty hard to ignore. It's just a clumsy way of trying to handle all of those different needs.

It's mostly about stopping them from consoling one another. You get a lot of that mutual support and planning if you put a bunch of them together. Scattering them out to different facilities or locking them in their own cells pretty much kills that off. The same logic applies to the off chance that something goes wrong. You are much less likely to see a riot or a group escape if the people in question aren't in one place.

You also have to think about the story you are telling the public. Folks outside the system have a pretty fixed idea that the worst of the lot is being locked away in some special and secure way. Providing that spectacle is a pretty big part of the whole arrangement. That is a lot of cost for what it ultimately accomplishes.

None of this was quite hammered out in one neat decision either. You got it built up over time from a bunch of local calls. That makes it a lot harder to take apart again.

You mostly need it to keep the whole thing from getting weird. If you put that group in with everyone else some of the general population would very likely kill one of them before the state got around to it. That would mess up the legal proceedings and give the extra person a way to get off. You get a similar problem if the group got together on their own, a bunch of people with nothing to lose is a pretty serious escape risk.

It also keeps the members from influencing one another or getting up to anything jointly. That isolation ends up having a pretty heavy psychological cost, which some folks say is part of the deal. You also end up with a population that needs a whole set of different medical, legal and psychological services that are a lot easier to furnish to a single group. None of that is really out to add to the sentence so much as to keep the legal process from breaking down before it gets to a finish line.

It's mostly about not letting the general population get away with lynching them. If you stuck a guy who'd already been condemned in with the rest you'd have to watch for every kind of reprisal. The guards themselves are also far likelier to get hurt trying to move such a person. Keeping that group in a separate unit lets you do both of those things with a much smaller staff. You get all of that without having to build a special kind of prison for one or two such cases.

That said the conditions that end up in place are a lot harsher than you'd see anywhere else. You've got decades of solitary confinement with almost no human contact. That isn't so much part of the sentence as it is something that just grew out of how the place happened to be set up. You end up with a lot of serious psychological damage as a result.

You've got a few practical reasons piling up on each other. First you have the obvious escape risk you'd get from having that many high stakes folks in one place. Put together for long enough and they've got time to get to know each other's routines. Nobody wants that. Then there's the question of the inmates themselves getting messed with. Most of the general population has a pretty clear idea of what to do in that situation. Isolation takes that possibility off the table.

You also run into a fair bit of legal bother. Quite a lot of the people who end up on that list will be called to the stand in someone else's case. You end up having to scramble to keep them from having any contact with the accused. Keeping them out of the way on a permanent basis is a lot easier than trying to manage that sort of thing case by case. None of that amounts to a philosophy really. The brutal conditions that tend to go with the setup are mostly the result of piling all of that practical caution on top of one another.

You've mostly got a legal mess to keep out of the general population. That kind of case bounces between the direct appeals process, state post conviction relief, and a shot at federal court. That whole cycle can gobble up twenty years. It's just a lot easier to keep legal records and schedules in a separate unit than to try to wrangle all that from inside the rest of the prison.

You are also managing some pretty extreme security risks on both ends. The person in question obviously has every motive to hurt others in retaliation and at the same time is very likely to get targeted by others inside. You can't really cabin both of those off in the general population.

The part that gets the least attention is the toll that kind of environment takes on a person. You have to cut human contact to a pretty brutal degree to keep the other two things from going wrong. That level of routine and isolation ends up doing a fair amount of damage to a person mentally. That is less something anyone wants and more something that happens in the process of doing the rest.

groups.question: How people program "Angry Birds"-like physics and collision detection.
texts:
You're almost certainly not writing the solver yourself. You'd grab box2d or box2d lite and feed it a bunch of shapes. That library handles the nasty iterative constraint stuff for you. Your actual job is the setup. You describe the pigs as dense static bodies, the birds as dynamic ones, and you fire the bird off by setting a linear velocity on the launch frame. You also need to squelch box2d's default angular velocity on that shot or the bird will spin out. Run the whole thing on a fixed time step, something like 120 hertz, and the integrator will stop exploding when a bunch of things hit at once.

The primitive tests inside that engine are nothing too mystical. A circle versus circle test is just a distance check against the sum of the two radii. You get a normal by taking a line from one center to the other. Circle against polygon is a bit more tedious since you have to find the closest point on each edge to the circle's center. Both of those emit a contact point along with a normal and a slightly negative distance. The constraint solver then takes that list and works at getting the overlap to zero over the course of a few iterations. That finite iteration count is what gets you the funny spongy wobble you see instead of a perfectly rigid response.

Getting the sound effects to line up is mostly an event based problem. You register a contact callback on the bodies and fire off a cluck whenever the collision force crosses some threshold. That keeps the noise from getting completely out of hand when a large structure finally gives way.

You end up using some off the shelf library for the heavy lifting, Box2D has been the standard for a long time. You describe all the boxes and circles and it handles the integration and solving. The part you actually write is the stuff around that. You set up a sweep and prune scheme to throw out pairs that have no chance of meeting. For the pairs that survive that first pass you check a circle against a line segment, which is basically a distance from a point to a line done a few times.

Once you have that contact it is mostly a matter of killing off the normal component of the velocity and letting the tangential one slide. You decide how much of the normal to kill with your coefficient of restitution, and the amount you shave off the tangential part with your friction constant. Getting it to feel right takes a lot of fiddling with those two numbers. You are far more likely to be tweaking constants by eye than fighting the math out. That back and forth is really the bulk of the work.

You're almost certainly building on top of Box2D. You've got it in virtually every game that looks like this, from the original down to the thousand clones. You slap a dynamic body on the bird and static ones on the terrain. Then you set up a whole bunch of different conditional filters so the right things hit the right other things. All the fun destruction stuff is really just you checking the impulse on a hit and, if it's big enough, simply deleting the block from the world. Stop updating it and the rest of the world stops recognizing it. The static things you leave behind will happily support the things on top of them.

You run out of the solver's patience pretty fast if a couple of these things get really badly wedged. The engine will just start to twitch, or worse, it will trap your bird inside a hole you weren't expecting. You end up needing to cheat a bit to keep the thing from getting stuck. That sort of thing is just part of the job. The whole system is also hopelessly sensitive to the numbers you pick at the start. You end up spending a great deal of time measuring things to arrive at numbers that feel roughly right.

You mostly pick up Box2D and bolt it on, since it was the standard for 2D work when most of that stuff got made. There is no secret geometry code for the birds hitting the pigs. The engine takes care of figuring out which shapes have met and then hands you a contact callback. That callback is where you go in and kill the thing that got hit. You do have to wait for the end of a time step to actually delete a body though. Yanking one out in the middle of a solve will leave the rest of the simulation in a mess.

Getting the right feel is almost entirely a matter of messing with the numbers. You want a high coefficient of restitution on the slingshot to get that sharp snap, and you want the birds themselves to be fairly bouncy. The band you drag on is just a distance constraint that you attach to the bird body. You let the player poke it around, the constraint objects to that, and then you let go. All the energy you got from the pull is already in the system to make the shot. It is the same trick you see in a bunch of other little contraptions.

You end up stacking a whole lot of other people's work. The actual math you write is mostly just gravity plus an initial velocity. Everything after the first hit gets handed off to a constraint solver, and that is almost always something like Box2D. You feed it shapes you have simplified to deadly extremes, a circle standing in for some very complicated bird design. Then you spend an absurd amount of time just twisting the restitution and friction numbers back and forth until a crash sounds right to your ear. There is no clean formula that gets you there.

That little dotted line you see while you are aiming is a bit of a cheat. You are just running the regular equations of motion out ahead of time to plot out a few points. You throw that preview away and let the real simulation take over only after you let go. If you tried to make the preview and the actual flight match in any more complicated way you would end up with a nightmare of mounting errors.

You end up leaning on some small open source library for the heavy lifting, Box2D being the usual one. You feed it the shapes for the birds, the blocks and the slingshot, and it keeps track of the whole mess. The library advances the world in very small fixed steps, which you have to decouple from your graphics frame rate. If you let one drive the other you get all these stuttering or slow motion moments. Getting that separation right is usually the hardest part.

Once the library figures out that two shapes are touching it does the projection to get them out of the overlap. It then looks at the direction they hit and bounces them off along that line. You can nudge the amount of that bounce around to get the result you want, a heavy wooden beam will bounce way less than a light painted target. When the sum of a blocks stress gets too high you just flag it for removal on the next step.

The funny part is that almost none of the fun you see in the finished game comes from the math. All the birds getting squished and the structures spinning wildly are mostly just some visual effects you slap on top to sell the impact. The simulation underneath is a lot drier than that.

The trajectory part is mostly boring. You set an initial velocity and let gravity do the rest, integrating position a frame at a time. There is one gotcha though. Do a big enough time step and a fast bird will pass right through a thin wall between two checks. You get around it by casting a line from where the bird was to where it's going and seeing whether any block lies along that line.

Collision is where the game lives. You don't model the whole structure as a general purpose set of rigid bodies, that's a nightmare to get right. Instead each block just keeps a health number. When the bird hits one you calculate an impulse from the bird's current speed and mass. Some of that goes into damage. The block type is just a lookup table for how much impulse it takes to pop. Wood next to a stone wall is only being protected while that stone wall is still around.

Once a block's health runs out you stop treating it as a solid thing. You swap it out for a bunch of little particles that draw on screen but block nothing. The bird then continues through the gap it has torn in and hits what was hidden behind. The structure takes care of its own disintegration from there. You put an equal limit on the bird so it eventually gives up and gets thrown away.

The whole thing ends up being a fairly tight loop of these two checks over and over. You aren't really scripting how the tower falls, you've just made the local rules that make it do so.

You keep a list of rigid bodies, each one with a position, a rotation, and some velocity. Every frame you run an integrator to move everything around and you need to pick a small enough time step or a fast sling shot bird will just pass clean through a wall. The integrator can be something simple like semi implicit Euler and that gets you pretty far. The wall of trouble is working out where the bodies touch. Most of the time you check one edge of a polygon against one of the other to get a pair of candidate axes. You push each shape out along those axes and the one with the smallest gap is the one you actually call a collision. Getting the pressure and the friction forces out of that contact is a decent amount of work on its own. It helps to run the whole contact resolution a dozen times in a row to let the bodies settle.

The trouble is that wooden planks are not static. Once you knock one off a stack the rest of the pile is going to be in constant flux. You either end up with a lot of jitter or the whole thing simply explodes. You usually have to manually tune how much correction you apply on each pass. It is more fiddling than real mathematics. Most of what you are doing is just trying to keep the number of bodies in constant contact from getting too large.

The fixed timestep part is the one that trips people up since you have to decouple that from the frame rate your graphics run at or you get all sorts of weird fast and slow motion.

You end up leaning on some small open source library for the heavy lifting, Box2D being the usual one. You feed it the shapes for the birds, the blocks and the slingshot, and it keeps track of the whole mess. The library advances the world in very small fixed steps, which you have to decouple from your graphics frame rate. If you let one drive the other you get all these stuttering or slow motion moments. Getting that separation right is usually the hardest part.

Once the library figures out that two shapes are touching it does the projection to get them out of the overlap. It then looks at the direction they hit and bounces them off along that line. You can nudge the amount of that bounce around to get the result you want, a heavy wooden beam will bounce way less than a light painted target. When the sum of a blocks stress gets too high you just flag it for removal on the next step.

The funny part is that almost none of the fun you see in the finished game comes from the math. All the birds getting squished and the structures spinning wildly are mostly just some visual effects you slap on top to sell the impact. The simulation underneath is a lot drier than that.

The user wants to know how you'd build Angry Birds-style physics. This isn't a game dev textbook question - they want the actual mechanics. Let me think about what's really going on.

You've got two main systems. The trajectory one is almost boring, it's just F=ma integrated each frame. Gravity pulls down, the initial velocity you set at launch carries the bird along a parabola. You sample the position each frame and check if it's hit anything. The integration step size matters though, if you go too long between checks a fast bird will tunnel right through a thin wall. You can work around that with a ray cast along the step instead of just point checks.

The collision part is where the fun is. You don't model every block as an individual rigid body in a general purpose engine. That gets way too messy. Instead you assign types. Wood breaks after a certain impulse hits it, stone takes a lot more, ice is light and shatters easily. You compute the impulse from the bird's velocity times mass and that number gets subtracted from the block's health. If health hits zero the block gets swapped from a solid collider to a set of little debris particles that no longer block other objects.

The whole thing naturally collapses into itself once enough blocks have been removed. You don't need any special logic for that, the integration and collision checks handle it. The bird keeps going through the gap it created and hits what's behind. The bird itself has some number of hits it can take before it stops being useful and gets replaced.

I should keep this to the actual mechanics rather than wandering off into engine recommendations or code. The user asked how people do it not which tools they reach for.
</think>

The trajectory part is mostly boring. You set an initial velocity and let gravity do the rest, integrating position a frame at a time. There is one gotcha though. Do a big enough time step and a fast bird will pass right through a thin wall between two checks. You get around it by casting a line from where the bird was to where it's going and seeing whether any block lies along that line.

Collision is where the game lives. You don't model the whole structure as a general purpose set of rigid bodies, that's a nightmare to get right. Instead each block just keeps a health number. When the bird hits one you calculate an impulse from the bird's current speed and mass. Some of that goes into damage. The block type is just a lookup table for how much impulse it takes to pop. Wood next to a stone wall is only being protected while that stone wall is still around.

Once a block's health runs out you stop treating it as a solid thing. You swap it out for a bunch of little particles that draw on screen but block nothing. The bird then continues through the gap it has torn in and hits what was hidden behind. The structure takes care of its own disintegration from there. You put an equal limit on the bird so it eventually gives up and gets thrown away.

The whole thing ends up being a fairly tight loop of these two checks over and over. You aren't really scripting how the tower falls, you've just made the local rules that make it do so.

The user wants to understand the actual engineering behind Angry Birds-style games. This isn't about game design or art — they're asking about the physics simulation and the collision detection that makes the whole thing work. I should get into the concrete stuff: how you represent the world, what integration method keeps things stable, and how you actually test for overlapping shapes.

The shape representation is the trickiest part. You can't just use bounding boxes because a pig sitting on a wooden plank needs to interact in ways a box in a box wouldn't. That means falling back on polygon collision, and for that you need to find the smallest separating axis. You also end up all tangled up in the order you process different contact points, because handling them out of sequence produces that awful jitter you see if you haven't been careful.

You're going to have to do a small sub-step for the actual movement calculation, and that's just a necessity if you don't want fast moving objects to pass clean right through the stuff they ought to be hitting. The whole thing comes together in a loop that runs over and over many times inside a single frame of animation.
</think>

You keep a list of rigid bodies, each one with a position, a rotation, and some velocity. Every frame you run an integrator to move everything around and you need to pick a small enough time step or a fast sling shot bird will just pass clean through a wall. The integrator can be something simple like semi implicit Euler and that gets you pretty far. The wall of trouble is working out where the bodies touch. Most of the time you check one edge of a polygon against one of the other to get a pair of candidate axes. You push each shape out along those axes and the one with the smallest gap is the one you actually call a collision. Getting the pressure and the friction forces out of that contact is a decent amount of work on its own. It helps to run the whole contact resolution a dozen times in a row to let the bodies settle.

The trouble is that wooden planks are not static. Once you knock one off a stack the rest of the pile is going to be in constant flux. You either end up with a lot of jitter or the whole thing simply explodes. You usually have to manually tune how much correction you apply on each pass. It is more fiddling than real mathematics. Most of what you are doing is just trying to keep the number of bodies in constant contact from getting too large.

groups.question: What makes the F-14 so loved and the F-35 so hated?
texts:
You're mostly looking at a couple of things. The Tomcat had a huge variable sweep wing that let it go from a subsonic cruiser to a high speed missile launcher in the same pass. You could see the whole idea of the airplane just by looking at it, and that kind of thing gets people's blood pumping. Add in thirty years of front line duty and that one Top Gun movie and you've got an object lesson in romance. The jet got to age out with some dignity too.

The new one had to optimize itself for not showing up on a scope and that process ended up with a pile of flat, odd looking surfaces. It looks like somebody built a plane out of building blocks with a padlock on top. Then you got stuck watching it get delayed over and over while it struggled to behave in the software sense. You can't exactly build up a warm feeling for an object that keeps letting you down. The movie they put out with the F-14 in the lead was a nice final little gloss to put on the old thing.

It's mostly a matter of what story each one got. The Tomcat had a thirty year run as the face of the carrier air wing before Top Gun took a pretty loose version of it and welded it to the national imagination. You end up with a whole generation that keeps a golden picture in their heads. Once the bird was finally grounded that memory just got polished up and put on a shelf. You get to grieve the loss of something that was already a myth.

The Joint Strike Fighter got billed to do the job of all those different types while keeping the price down. It has spent the last couple decades in the middle of that process getting out of its own way. A long public string of bugs and cost overruns doesn't give you much to cheer for. The awkward little looks of the stealth shaping don't help either since they don't fit the existing hero template. You can't really build a legend around something that is still being worked out.

The actual technical merits of the two don't come in all that far apart. You've got an old dog that got to keep a hero's halo and a new one that got to wear all its own mistakes on its sleeve.

It's mostly a matter of the stories people got to tell. You've got the Tomcat locked in as this almost mythic thing from Top Gun. Nobody out there to prove that out in the real world after it got retired. You just got to keep polishing that image. The III is still sitting in the middle of this absolutely massive and extremely badly managed program. Every little hiccup gets written up. It also got asked to do the job of three different birdso at once which is a recipe for the sort of endless teething problems you kept reading about. Would either of them get the same treatment if the roles were swapped. The Tomcat would have run out of cones to avoid before it got retired as well.

That isn't to say the problems on the later plane aren't actually there. They are. They just got to get a front row seat to the whole thing unfold. You get to judge the former on the basis of a couple of really good movies and a little bit of fact.

It's mostly a matter of what you got to see. You got a whole decade of Top Gun reruns painting the Tomcat as some kind of silver bullet. That movie froze the plane in a heroic 1980s light and nobody has thought to update their opinion. It was also a big, loud, visible cold war artifact that fit a very simple idea of what a fighter ought to be. The F 35 got stuck living in the opposite set of narratives. It kept blowing up the budget and missing every single date. You also can't get attached to something that hides all of its real cleverness from public view. That much of it is secretly quite capable doesn't help a thing.

You are also comparing two planes that got into the public eye under entirely different sets of circumstances. One arrived with a lot of commercial hype and the other has had to live out its existence under a cloud of endless bureaucratic failure. You are really arguing about a old and very good movie versus a long and very unseemly record of government mistakes. The actual machines have very little to do with the whole thing.

It's mostly a problem of what stories people got to hear. Top Gun handed the Hornet a perfectly coherent legend and the public just happily adopted it. You saw the thing do exactly what the movie claimed it could. The whole myth was checked out by the reality behind it. The Joint Strike Fighter on the other hand has spent the last two decades as nothing but a running series of delay stories. You got an endless parade of cost overruns and bugs to read about and none of the romantic hardware to take your mind off them. At that point resentment is a pretty natural reaction.

The two also wed very different ideas of what a fighter ought to look like. The variable geometry wings on the older bird gave it a shape you could easily recognize and admire. You got all sorts of good angles to work with. The new plane is built to dodge that very sort of attention. It's a blocky shape that is actively unimpressive to the eye. You can't very well build up a mythology around something that has no business being seen in the first place.

It's mostly a matter of what posters got to see. You got a couple of decades of Tom Cruise screaming at friends while he flew the Tomcat. That film pretty much wrote the plane into legend for anyone who never got to see it in person. The whole thing got retired while all that cool stuff was still fresh in the popular mind. Nobody had to sit through the endless maintenance that made it such a beast to keep in the air.

You don't get that same benefit with the new plane. The whole program has been a series of publicly documented delays, cost overruns, and botched parts. You are essentially watching the construction of the thing in real time and getting to see every error. If you had to follow the Tomcat through its long and difficult service that same way the sentiment would almost certainly be a lot more sour. You're comparing a finished and very good story to one that's still a real pain to put together.

You're mostly hearing the complaints from the guys who fly them. The Tomcat has that visual drama you don't get anywhere else, the wings actually sweep back and forth right in front of you. The Joint Strike Fighter is a weird bird like blob that looks underpowered and badly proportioned, that huge radome ruins the whole front end. Those are the sorts of things that get picked apart in the hangar. The contract for the new model was so vast that every single snafu got written up as some kind of massive failure. With the old planes the teething problems just got written off as the price of doing business. You also have the fact that the last of the old model only recently went on the way out, so they've had time to take on a bit of a mythic character.

That said the new model has been in service long enough now that some of the worst of the grumbling has died down. You'd still get a lot of the same griping from the aircrew you next to either one though.

You mostly got the Tomcat in a finished form. You saw it rip around in movies and that's what stuck in your head. The whole thing got soaked in the kind of mythology that only comes after the fact. By the time they were junking the last of the birds you had a pretty good childhood memory to grieve. You can't really hate a thing you've already built a fairy tale around.

The 35 you have to watch in the making and the making has been an endless series of screw ups. Every single cost overrun and delay gets hashed out by the press so the plane has got to a point where it is practically synonymous with mismanagement. They've also got to stretch one design to satisfy the needs of the navy and the air force and a dozen allies and the result is something that appears to satisfy nobody. You can't build up much of a mythology in a state of perpetual and unending bad news.
